tom_tat: This volume is selected and translated from the Chinese Buddhist Records of Pure Land Saints, a collection of nearly a thousand accounts of rebirth in the Pure Land through Buddha-recitation, presented here as models and encouragement for practitioners, with emphasis on recent accounts from the Republican era.
noi_dung:
Foreword

This volume has been selected and translated by the author from the original Chinese Buddhist work, the Records of Pure Land Saints. That collection was compiled under the Qing dynasty, in the reign of Qianlong, by the layman Peng Tesheng together with his nephew Xisu, who gathered accounts of people who attained rebirth in the Pure Land through Buddha-recitation. Toward the end of the Daoguang reign, the layman Hu Ding of Lian'gui collected further accounts of rebirth and continued the compilation. Then, in the era of the Republic of China, Dharma Master Desen gathered additional verified accounts of Pure Land practice and supplemented the work. Altogether, from first to last, there are nearly a thousand stories.

In truth, those who have practiced the Pure Land teaching and attained rebirth are far more numerous than that. The old records concerning the Pure Land were partly lost, the chronicles were incomplete, and in former days communication was inconvenient, so accounts of rebirth through Buddha-recitation were never widely circulated nor fully recorded. Consider the scenes when Master Shandao was at Chang'an and Master Shaokang was at Xinding, when the sound of Buddha-recitation filled every street: one may be sure that those reborn in the Pure Land numbered more than tens of millions. Still, the accounts collected here may serve well enough as models for Pure Land practitioners of later generations.

Some years ago, the author had recorded several dozen accounts of rebirth through Buddha-recitation in Vietnam, but they were regrettably lost during the upheavals of war. Hence I have had to present these Chinese accounts of rebirth as examples to encourage Pure Land practitioners. In this volume I have selected and translated only the most remarkable accounts from the original work, fearing that too many would weary the reader. Earlier, Venerable Van Duc (Thich Tri Tinh) translated about one third of the collection under the title The Road to the Land of Bliss, which many readers cherished. Several fellow practitioners asked me to continue that work and to translate accounts of lay practitioners of recent times, so that people of our own day might follow in their footsteps. For that reason, this volume gives special attention to stories from the recent Republican era.

The words and deeds of the saints and sages who practiced the Pure Land teaching in former times are like music and bright mirrors that encourage and illuminate fellow practitioners. An ancient author once wrote a Pure Land book entitled Sounds of the Lotus Hour: the lotus hour refers to the lotus clock of the White Lotus Society of Master Huiyuan, and the sounds are the pure melodies that urge all beings to recite the Buddha's name. Following that intention, I have entitled this volume MELODIES OF THE PURE LOTUS.

Every school, besides its doctrine, has its record of lived experience and practice. Practice both confirms doctrine and stands as a bright mirror that reminds and encourages practitioners. This volume is a historical testimony confirming that the Land of Bliss truly exists and that the merit of Buddha-recitation brings benefit both in this present life and at the hour of death. Since the Land of Bliss truly exists, it follows that the heavens, the hells, the three realms and six destinies, the law of cause and effect in matters of wrongdoing and blessing, and the realms of saints, spirits, and ghosts are likewise all real and not illusory. Reflecting deeply and broadly upon this point, one will surely be able to cut off evil, turn away from wrongdoing, and incline toward the wholesome path.

"Leaning on my desk, I gaze upon the ancients;

Catching my shadow in the mirror, I ponder the affairs of life."

I hope that readers of this volume, awakening to the truth that this life is suffering and impermanence, will soon resolve to seek liberation, cultivate wholesome blessings, keep a vegetarian diet, and recite the Buddha's name. Beginning with self-cultivation and then urging relatives and all others to practice, even though this world has not yet become the Land of Bliss, still within each region and locality there will be much blessing, benefit, and peace.

Moreover, the details throughout this volume may guide the reader to profound and subtle meanings, like chewing sugarcane from the tip down to the root: one will gradually enter ever deeper stages of realization.

LIEN DU

—oOo—

tom_tat: Great Master Hoang Te, who calmed the sea dikes by mantra power and devoted his old age to Buddha-recitation; Great Master De Qing (Old Man Hanshan), who awakened at Mount Wutai, suffered exile, and taught the Pure Land gate; and Dharma Master Di Xian, restorer of the Tiantai school, who lectured widely, practiced daily recitation, and passed away peacefully in 1932 amid supporting recitation.
noi_dung:
HOANG TE

Great Master Hoang Te, of the Yao family, styled Dongzhou, was a native of Yuyao. As a small child he already wore his hair in tufts while dwelling at Baoji Temple in his village. At sixteen he fully shaved his head and received the novice precepts, and at the age of twenty he received the complete precepts.

The Master strictly observed the precepts and studied the Tiantai doctrinal meditation under Dharma Master Benshan Quan. Before long his study had reached a point of penetrating mastery. He regularly practiced repentance rites such as those of the Pure Land, the Lotus Sutra, and the Golden Light Sutra. One day in meditation, he saw the Venerable Siming present him with a wish-fulfilling rhinoceros-horn scepter, after which his eloquence flowed forth like a gushing spring.

Under the Yuan dynasty, in the first year of the Taiding era, he was invited to preside over Yuanjue Temple in Wanshou county. The following year, in the nearby county of Yanguan, violent storms arose and the sea dikes were about to be breached by the waves; the people of the whole region trembled in fear. The Grand Chancellor Toghon also grew anxious and had the local officials earnestly invite the Master to the sea dikes to establish a great Water and Land assembly for prayer. When he arrived, he entered the Loving-Kindness samadhi, recited the Great Compassion Mantra over sea sand, and scattered it along the embankment. Wherever his feet tread, the dikes were made firm, and the wind and waves gradually calmed until they ceased entirely. Everyone praised it as miraculous! Afterward the Master successively presided over the great monasteries of Jiqing, Xianci, and Binjiang. In old age he returned to Baoji Temple in his homeland and devoted himself to the Buddha-Recitation samadhi.

In the sixteenth year of the Zhizheng era, on the third day of the tenth month, the Master felt slightly ill. He summoned his disciples and instructed them on the meaning of the Mind-Only Pure Land. When some in the assembly did not yet understand, he raised his voice and sternly rebuked them, saying: "The shore of birth and death is most perilous and affords no place to rest in peace. Why are you still not awakened?". Having spoken, he joined his palms, recited the Buddha's name, and passed away.

DE QING

Great Master De Qing, styled Chengyin, in later life took the name Old Man Hanshan. He was of the Cai family of Jinling. His mother dreamed that Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva carried a young boy in her arms and presented him to her, and thus she conceived him. When he was born, he was wrapped in two white coverings. At nineteen he left the household life and devoted himself to Buddha-recitation. One night the Master dreamed that Amitabha appeared in the sky toward the setting sun. The Buddha's features were clear, radiant, and majestic, and from then on that vision often appeared before him. He then went to Mount Wutai, where through meditation he awakened to his original mind, and vowed to copy the Avatamsaka Sutra in his own blood, reciting the Buddha's name with every stroke of the brush. After long practice, stillness and activity became as one.

In the tenth year of the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, the Master settled at Mount Lao. The Empress Dowager Li, hearing of his virtue and admiring him, provided funds to have a monastery built for him there, bestowing the plaque Haiyin Temple. At that time the Empress Dowager often sent eunuch officials to build and repair temples and stupas in various places. Among the powerful there were those who bore a grudge against the eunuch officials and plotted with a group of Taoist priests of the Eastern Depot to beat drums and submit accusations, claiming that he had seized Taoist cloisters and converted them into Buddhist temples. The affair implicated the Master: he was stripped of his monastic robes and exiled to Leizhou. When bidding farewell to the assembly, he remained serene and wrote a verse expressing his resolve:

The kasaya cast off, exchanged for common dress,

Wherever I may go is a place of the Way!

Though I meet conditions like burning fire,

How could a heart of ice and snow melt away?

Wherever he went, the Master still expounded the Dharma in lay dress, and vowed to propagate the Mahayana sutras, composing commentaries on works such as the Shurangama, the Lankavatara, and the Complete Enlightenment Sutra. In the forty-second year of Wanli, he received an imperial pardon restoring him to the monastic order. On his way back, passing Mount Lu, he delighted in its pure and secluded scenery and built a hut beneath Five-Nipple Peak. Following the example of Master Huiyuan, he dug a lotus pond, divided the hours of the day for Pure Land practice, and cultivated with great diligence.

At that time a Zen practitioner of Haiyang, while seeking to receive the precepts, asked about the essential meaning of the Pure Land. The Master said: "The World Honored One taught many skillful means of practice for leaving the round of birth and death and advancing toward Buddhahood. Foremost among them is the gate of reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, which the Buddha taught unasked by anyone — enough to show how momentous it is! This gate embraces all three capacities and gathers in all four assemblies; it is not a provisional device set up only for those of dull capacity. The sutra says: 'To purify the Buddha-land, first purify your own mind!' Therefore Pure Land practitioners must take the purification of the mind as their foundation. To purify the mind, what is most necessary is to keep the precepts pure and undefiled. Though the precepts are many, in essence they are nothing beyond the three karmas of body, the four karmas of speech, and the three karmas of mind. Keeping these ten karmas pure and wholesome is the true cause for avoiding the three evil destinies. With a mind thus purified by keeping the precepts, give rise to compassion, renounce the filth and suffering of the Saha world, vow to be reborn in the Land of Bliss in order swiftly to attain the fruit of the Way and deliver oneself and all sentient beings — and establish Buddha-recitation as the principal practice. The manner of Buddha-recitation may follow each person's capacity and circumstances, but it must be done with a true mind and true practice to bring genuine results!".

A layman named Pure Mind came to request instruction and asked: "Why are there so many people who recite the Buddha's name without diligence and find it hard to bring it into a single unbroken mass?". The Master instructed him: "The foremost essential of practice is an earnest resolve to escape the suffering of birth, death, and rebirth. Without an earnest concern for this, how could one recite the Buddha's name diligently and bring it into a single mass? Since beginningless kalpas, sentient beings have let every thought follow deluded fancy, and the root of attachment runs deep. Even in the human realm there is little joy and much suffering, while in the round of rebirth, birth in the human and heavenly realms is as rare as earth on a fingernail, and falling into the three evil destinies is as common as earth upon the great ground! The ancients said: 'Once fallen into the three destinies for a thousand myriad kalpas, when will a human body be regained?' If in this life one does not grieve deeply over the suffering of birth, death, and rebirth, but lets every thought follow defiled emotion, and hopes with a shallow faith to recite the Buddha's name and gain liberation, it is like hoping to save a thousand cartloads of blazing fire with a single ladle of water! Practicing in this way, one may fear that once this human body is lost it will be hard to regain, and a moment's negligence will be regretted for long ages! Therefore resolve upon diligence, use Buddha-recitation to break through myriad deluded thoughts, and in every time and place keep the Buddha's name present before you. Determinedly applying such earnest and painful effort, in time it will become ripe and harmonious, and the recitation will naturally form a single mass. All this depends on one's own reflection and wholehearted exertion. If the Buddha's name is made a mere outward form, there is surely no hope of attaining rebirth and liberation!".

After some years at Mount Lu, the Master moved to Caoxi. In the tenth month of the third year of the Tianqi era, he felt slightly ill and told others: "This old monk's worldly karma is nearly exhausted!". He then bathed, burned incense, sat upright, and passed away. At that moment a dazzling light filled the sky. The Master lived seventy-eight years.

DI XIAN

Dharma Master Di Xian, whose Dharma name was Gu Xu and style Zhuosan, of the Zhou family, was a native of Huangyan in Zhejiang province. Endowed with planted wisdom and complete wholesome roots, at twenty he left the household life at Baiyun Temple in Linhai county. Two years later he received the complete precepts at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai.

From then on he studied meditation in winter and the teachings in summer, practicing the Way with diligence. He drew close to eminent elders and was especially intimate with Old Man Minxi. He once attended a lecture series on the Lotus Sutra, and before hearing it through had already grasped the subtle meaning of the Three Truths and three contemplations. He was then asked to take the small seat and repeat the lecture; his exposition was profound and his reasoning penetrating, so that his fellow students were all startled and admiring. Venerable Min also sighed in praise, calling him a mighty pillar of the Dharma gate. At twenty-eight, the Master opened a Lotus Sutra assembly at Liutong Temple in Hangzhou. When expounding the passage on "opening the Buddha's knowledge and vision," he suddenly entered samadhi and sat in silence. A moment later he emerged from meditation and continued; his eloquence was unobstructed, answering objections and resolving doubts like water pouring from a vase, his speech opening and closing with a freedom none could restrain. From then on he regularly took the propagation of the Dharma and the benefit of beings as his responsibility. Fearing that much wisdom and little meditative stability would obstruct the Way, he sealed himself in retreat at the Holy Fruit Hermitage of Cixi Temple, studying the Mahayana scriptures in his spare hours.

Three years later, upon emerging from retreat, he at once accepted an invitation to lecture on the Lotus Sutra at Longhua Temple in Shanghai. When the series was finished he returned to Jinshan Monastery to practice Zen, then went to Guoqing Temple to practice contemplation. Through that period his understanding grew ever more profound and subtle, and Patriarch Shi Duanrong chose him as the forty-third generation heir of the Tiantai school. For more than twenty years afterward he responded to unceasing invitations to lecture everywhere, seldom idle, holding Dharma assemblies numbering in the thousands. Each day the Master recited the Diamond Sutra, the Complete Enlightenment Sutra, the Contemplation of Immeasurable Life Sutra, and the Vows of Samantabhadra, and recited the Buddha's name more than ten thousand times as his daily course. On the full moon and new moon he additionally recited the Brahma Net Sutra.

In a lifetime of teaching, he restored Tou Tuo Temple in Wenzhou, Wannian Temple on Mount Tiantai, Guanzong Temple in Ningbo, and Fantian Temple in Hangzhou. He also founded a Buddhist academy to train monastic talent and established pure cloisters for the assembly to practice. Guanzong Temple was the Master's permanent residence. His writings and instructions were numerous: below, they accorded with the capacities of his hearers; above, they deeply agreed with the Buddha's truth, so that monastics and laity alike received moistening benefit. His method of instruction expounded Tiantai doctrine while practicing Pure Land conduct, so that whenever he lectured on the sutras he always concluded by directing his hearers to Buddha-recitation. The Master himself truly practiced in that same way, perfect in both understanding and conduct, admired by all and honored as the restorer of the Tiantai teaching of his time. In matters of public benefit and charity he was likewise generous in lending his aid to their success.

In the spring and summer of the Xinwei year of the Republic, the Master lectured at Jade Buddha Temple in Shanghai. He also responded to the invitation of the laymen of Wuxi by expounding Master Jing'an's text on arousing the bodhi-mind.
Being advanced in age, oppressed by hot weather, and wearied by excessive Buddhist duties, the Master fell ill after the lecture series. Upon returning to his home temple, his spirits and appetite declined day by day. He therefore cut off all involvements and resolved to devote himself to Buddha-recitation, seeking rebirth. In the summer of the Renshen year, he entrusted the procedures and regulations of Guanzong Temple in full, designating his disciple Baojing to continue the work of propagation.

On the second day of the seventh month, before noon, the Master suddenly joined his palms, faced west, and sat quietly for a moment, then said: "Amitabha has come to escort me; this old man now bids you farewell!". He then asked his attendants to prepare fragrant water for his bath. After changing into fresh clean robes and donning his kasaya, he asked to be helped to the main hall to venerate the Buddha, then asked to be assisted down and to sit in lotus posture within the jeweled shrine. Next, he had the assembly recite the Buddha's name in unison. He spoke a brief parting verse:

Through Buddha-recitation,

The Pure Land stands before me.

Truly receiving its benefit,

Strive on diligently, all of you!

At one hour and three quarters past noon, he peacefully passed away with a smile amid the supporting recitation of the great assembly. The Master's countenance appeared very bright and fresh, and some hours later the crown of his head was still warm. This was the second day of the seventh month in the twenty-first year of the Republic (1932). The Master lived seventy-five years, with fifty-five monastic years. His remains were enshrined by his disciples in a stupa at Cixi, Mount Wulei.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Venerable Tho Tam, the Barefoot Great Master, who strictly kept the precepts, devoted himself to Buddha-recitation, prayed successfully for rain, and passed away seated in lotus posture together with the dog and cat he had sheltered, in the Guangxu era.
noi_dung:
THO TAM

Venerable Tho Tam, styled Chuyen Tay, of the Mao family, was a native of Fangcheng in eastern Zhejiang. From birth he took only plain and simple food, never using milk, meat, or fish. Grown up, he grew weary of the dusty world and resolved to leave secular life and cultivate the Way. At eighteen he entered Xiaoling Mountain Temple west of the city and, under Dharma Master Gioi Am, shaved his head and left the household life.

When he was about to receive the complete precepts, Master Gioi Am fell gravely ill. Tho Tam reflected: "The propagation of the Buddha's teaching depends on venerable elders such as my teacher. Compared with that, my own body, fragile as morning dew, is hardly worth cherishing!". So he prepared fragrant water, bathed, went before the Three Jewels, burned incense and made a vow, then returned to his room and cut open his own belly, intending to slice off a piece of his liver to mix with medicine to cure his teacher. But no sooner had he drawn the knife lightly across his belly than, seized by agonizing pain, he fell fainting to the ground. After a while he revived and crawled back to his bed; by then the eastern sky was already bright. The assembly discovered him and hastened to bind his wound with medicine and bandages. When Master Gioi Am learned of it, he summoned Tho Tam and comforted him, saying: "Your filial devotion is strong indeed, but it is by no means the proper conduct of a practitioner. Moreover, I myself know the season and conditions: since birth is fundamentally unborn, what is there that perishes? What you did sprang entirely from deluded fancy. Yet out of pity for one sincere thought of filial devotion, I shall linger on a little while!". Sure enough, about a month after Tho Tam had received the complete precepts and returned, Master Gioi Am passed away. Tho Tam, filial by nature, grieved beyond measure and arranged the encoffining and burial with meticulous care in every detail.

Before long, he entrusted the temple's affairs to his Dharma brother Lien Duong and journeyed to study in various places. He strictly observed the precepts, practiced the ascetic disciplines, went barefoot and bareheaded, wearing but a single robe in winter and summer, and constantly devoted himself to Buddha-recitation. Seeing this, people called him the Barefoot Great Master. In the autumn of the Xinsi year of the Guangxu era, Tho Tam returned to Xiaoling Mountain Temple. At that time a long drought had parched the land, and the villages round about had all set up altars to pray for rain. The district magistrate, Magistrate Ton, was anxiously heartsick, praying day and night without response. Moved by compassion, Tho Tam went straight to see him, comforted him not to grieve excessively, and took the responsibility of praying for rain upon himself. The next day, a Renzi day, he took his bowl to a dried-up ravine stream and recovered an object shaped like a gecko. On the Yimao day, Tho Tam established an altar, recited mantras, and made obeisance through the six periods. In the Yin hour of the Bingchen day, rain fell from the sky but stopped after a few moments. Magistrate Ton sent the local gentry, led by Mr. Ly Tieu Nham, to request further prayers. The Master said: "Do not worry, gentlemen; tomorrow there will be heavy rain!". That night Tho Tam sincerely recited mantras and prayed, bowing in homage until dawn. Sure enough, at the noon hour of the Dingsi day, rain poured down as if overturned from buckets until evening, and the fields were filled brimful with water. The people of the region rejoiced. Magistrate Ton led the gentry up the mountain to give thanks. The magistrate, observing the manners of a disciple, personally wrote four large characters, "Eight Dragons Bestow Blessings," to commemorate the event. The Master remained calm and tranquil, showing nothing unusual. Magistrate Ton sighed: "Only now do I know how profound monastic virtue is — beyond conception!".

In the autumn of the Renwu year, Tho Tam closed his retreat hut, cutting off all involvements. Each day he recited the Great Compassion Mantra one hundred and eight times and the Buddha's name one hundred thousand times. In addition he recited the names of Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta a thousand times, and bowed thirty times each to the Buddha Shakyamuni of the present and to the Three Holy Ones of the West. In his hut he kept a dog and a cat, for whom he daily administered refuge and prayers. Because of this, the cat would not catch mice and the dog would not eat filth. After three years, on the nineteenth day of the ninth month, he emerged from retreat. At the beginning of the eleventh month, Tho Tam caught a light dysentery for a few days and recovered. But from then on his body gradually weakened. The monks took turns attending him, but he would not allow it, saying: "As renunciates, each of us has his own course of practice; we must not cause one another to neglect it. If the time truly comes, I shall have someone call for you!". On the evening of the twenty-sixth, Tho Tam summoned his disciples to his bedside and instructed them: "Tonight I shall return to the West; quickly bring fragrant water!". After shaving his head, bathing, and changing his robes, he sat in lotus posture, intoned the hymn of praise to the Buddha, and bade the assembly join in. After reciting the Buddha's name for more than a hundred utterances, his voice grew gradually fainter and his head bowed slightly. Suddenly he raised his head upright and said: "I am going! Take care, all of you!". Then, loudly reciting the Buddha's name once more, he passed away. That night the dog and cat kept in the hut likewise sat upright and passed away. Everyone said they had followed the Master in rebirth.

This was in the Yiyou year of the Guangxu era.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Venerable Tu Ngan, who recited sixty thousand Buddha-names daily, foresaw the exact day of his rebirth, visited the West in samadhi and returned to urge the assembly to practice diligently before passing away lying on his right side.
noi_dung:
TU NGAN

Venerable Tu Ngan, styled Nguyen Dang, of the Ta family, was a native of Qiantang at Hangzhou. In youth he studied Confucianism and ranked among the licentiates. Before long, feeling the impermanence of worldly affairs, he took refuge in the Three Jewels and traveled to study under good spiritual teachers of both Zen and the doctrinal schools. Later, hearing Dharma Master Ngoc Phong teach: "To seek escape from suffering, there is no easier gate to accomplishment than Buddha-recitation," he resolved to recite sixty thousand utterances of the Buddha's name daily as his fixed course. Whatever merit he made in life, he dedicated toward the Pure Land. In the Renshen year of the Tongzhi era, he further resolved to receive the five precepts at Haichao Temple.

In the ninth year of Guangxu, weary of the dusty world and longing for early liberation, he entrusted his household to his two sons and went straight to Huguo Temple, where he asked Abbot Kinh Phong to shave his head. That winter he received the complete precepts at Qiyuan Temple on Zhong Mountain. He then returned to Huguo Temple to cultivate the pure karma with single purpose. Through long and exhausting effort, Tu Ngan gradually fell ill; though treated many times, the illness would heal only to return. His two sons, missing him dearly, brought him home to convalesce, setting aside a quiet room as his place of secluded practice. In the autumn of the fifteenth year of Guangxu, he suddenly contracted dysentery, and medicine proved ineffective. From then on, though his food and drink steadily diminished, his recitation grew ever more reverent and earnest. On the tenth day of the ninth month, Tu Ngan called his two sons and said: "The hour of my rebirth has come. Go and invite the monks to come to the house and recite the Buddha's name for seven days, to escort me to the West!". He fixed the early morning of the twelfth as the start of the seven-day retreat, telling the monk Lang Phong that he would remain only seven more days. On the full-moon day, taking the hand of his Dharma friend Dinh Son, he said: "Only three days more, and I shall return to the Land of Bliss!".

On the night of the seventeenth, in the fourth watch, he asked the hour; his sons answered that it was the Chou hour. Tu Ngan said: "The Chou hour means the eighteenth day has already begun — the appointed date of my rebirth. Invite the monks to chant the sacred name in support!". As the assembly voiced the Buddha's name, he recited along. After about half a stick of incense, he suddenly fell silent and closed his eyes. After a while he abruptly opened his eyes, joined his palms, thanked the monks, and said: "I have already reached the West and paid homage to Amitabha and the two great bodhisattvas. The Buddha in his compassion bestowed a pure robe upon me, and Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva with a willow branch sprinkled sweet dew upon my head. Gazing afar, I saw Great Master Lianchi expounding the Dharma to the assembly of superior good persons. Roaming over the vast jeweled pond, looking across the precious lotus blossoms, I saw one lotus throne inscribed with the name of my own rebirth. The Buddha told me to return temporarily to the Saha world and announce to everyone that I have been reborn in the Pure Land. I earnestly urge you all to practice Buddha-recitation diligently, so that one day we may meet together in the Lotus Land!". Having spoken, he asked for cool water, drank three sips, lay down on his right side, recited the Buddha's name some dozens of times, and passed away.

The next day, at the encoffining, the crown of his head was still warm.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Zen Master Chi Thien, who turned to the Pure Land so that a whole mountain region took up Buddha-recitation, with the wondrous departures of the storekeeper Cam Phong and of Master Mac Am, who held sixty thousand recitations daily and passed away facing west in the twenty-eighth year of Guangxu.
noi_dung:
CHI THIEN

Zen Master Chi Thien lived under the Qing; his origins are not clearly known. During the Tongzhi and Guangxu years, he spread the teaching at Haihui Temple on Mount Lu. His virtue was lofty, and the four assemblies revered and gathered around him; he was a renowned worthy of Jiangxi in recent times.

After penetrating the mind-essence, he turned to Buddha-recitation, taking the Pure Land as the refuge both for his own practice and for his exhortation of others. Thus in those days the villagers of that mountain region all wore rosaries and every household enshrined the Buddha. From farmers and artisans to woodcutters and cowherds, when free from work many could be seen sitting beneath a tree or upon a rock, eyes closed, reciting the Buddha's name — a common sight no one found strange. That legacy is still handed down today.

In old age the Zen Master entrusted the temple to his senior disciple, Abbot Thanh Hu, and dwelled in a quiet hut devoted to practice. When students entered the hut to seek instruction, he bade them sit at ease and answered each according to capacity. There was a monk named Cam Phong, storekeeper in charge of the monastery's provisions, who each day also planted vegetables, chopped firewood, practiced meditation, and recited the Buddha's name; the assembly regarded him as an ordinary person. One year, at the beginning of winter, he came to the abbot's quarters to resign his post. Abbot Thanh Hu instructed him: "The monastery has just begun its Buddha-recitation retreat; do not leave so soon. Stay through the end of the year, then go!". He replied: "My time has come; I cannot wait!". The Abbot said: "I shall hold it back for you!". Cam Phong bowed in thanks and withdrew. In spring, on the third day of the new year, he came again to ask leave. The Abbot said: "If you leave at the new year, the assembly will be stirred; wait a few more days!". Cam Phong withdrew once more.

On the tenth day, he went to the abbot's quarters and firmly requested leave, saying: "I have lived long together with my fellow practitioners and feel deep affection for them. After the Lantern Festival, most of the monks will scatter to wander in all directions, and there will be no further chance to meet. So I wish my fellow companions to accompany me part of the way!". Hearing this, the Abbot consented. Cam Phong bowed in thanks, then went to pay respects to Master Chi Thien. The Zen Master, foreknowing, had prepared a cup of clear water and instructed his attendant: "If Storekeeper Cam comes, tell him to drink this cup of water; he need not come in for an audience.". The attendant conveyed the message, and Cam Phong reverently drank. At noon he still took the meal with the assembly. After the meal, the Abbot announced to the assembly: "Storekeeper Cam is about to journey far. Two hours after noon, I ask the whole assembly to don robes, bring small wooden bells and chimes, and come to his hut to see him off!". Hearing this, most were bewildered and puzzled. At the appointed hour, the precentor led the monks there. Cam Phong had already swept his hut clean and empty; in the center stood an incense altar with a Buddha image, with seats arranged on both sides for the assembly. When the Abbot arrived, Cam Phong bowed low, then prostrated before the monks. Abbot Thanh Hu kindly spoke a verse of Dharma entrustment. Only then did the assembly realize that the storekeeper was about to pass away to the West. After the Abbot withdrew, the precentor intoned the Amitabha Sutra, and Cam Phong, seated in his place, chanted along. When the chant passed to the hymn and turned to Buddha-recitation, after the incense had burned about an inch further, his voice grew fainter, and the rosary in his hand fell to the mat. The monk seated nearby felt for his breath and signaled that the storekeeper had breathed his last. The assembly dared not disturb him and continued reciting as before. After a while, Cam Phong suddenly opened his eyes and asked the monks to take turns in supporting recitation for a full day and night. Having spoken, he closed his eyes and departed directly.

In the Wuxu year of the Guangxu era, the court changed to new policies. Master Chi Thien lamented: "The age of the Dharma's decline has come, and I am old and cannot save it! I only wish to be swiftly reborn in the Land of Bliss, and after realizing the fruit of Non-arising, to return to this world to protect the true teaching!". Having spoken, he wrote farewell letters to eminent monks everywhere. Abbot Thanh Hu was then presiding over Yuantong Temple at Nanchang; receiving the letter, he hastened back. As the Abbot stepped into the monastery, Master Chi Thien was still seated leaning on his desk,
writing his final instructions. Seeing the Abbot, the Zen Master finished his business, smiled, and said: "Every great matter I entrust entirely to you. I am going!". Having spoken, seated upright upon his seat, he passed away.

MAC AM

Great Master Mac Am, Dharma name Thuong Nhan, styled Chan Nguyen, of the Zhou family, was a native of Hengzhou in Hunan. His father, a Confucian scholar, died early. As a boy the Master was bright and quick; a glance sufficed for him to read through several lines. At fifteen his literary talent far surpassed his companions, and his teacher thought his future official career would surely be brilliant. For the next two years he lodged at Yanfeng Temple to study, where, copying the Diamond Sutra, he came upon the line "the past, present, and future mind are all ungraspable" and suddenly gave rise to the thought of leaving the world.

In the seventh year of Xianfeng, when his mother sought to arrange a marriage for him, he secretly fled to Nanfeng Temple and left the household life under Zen Master Pho Chieu. The next year he received the precepts from Venerable Thuy Dinh at Phuoc Nghiem Temple. Hearing that Zen Master Chuc Thanh Luong's teaching flourished greatly, he went to receive the mind-seal. The following year he called upon Dharma Master Phap Van and penetrated deeply into the teachings, by which even the Confucian books became thoroughly clear to him. Renowned scholars who heard of the Master all delighted to seek his company. Vigorous in the upward path, he hid himself at Ky Cung Rock on the Southern Peak, where together with Dharma Master Thiem Van they encouraged one another in earnest practice.

In the Tongzhi years, the Master traveled to call upon eminent elders north and south, awakened to the source of mind, then returned to Phuoc Nghiem Temple to read the Great Canon. In the autumn of the second year of Guangxu, he built a hut beside Chuc Thanh Temple on the Southern Peak and cultivated in painful, secret effort; with time his realization grew ever deeper. From then on all secular books were thoroughly mastered, and famous scholars again sought his company as before. Dai Thien Temple on the Southern Peak, originally an ancient shrine, had been seized by others; the Master raised funds to redeem and restore it. Modeling its rule on that of Zen Master Che Wu, monks from the ten directions gathered like clouds until there was not room to contain them. All students there penetrated nature and characteristics and kept a dignified discipline. The Master used Tiantai doctrinal meditation as the vanguard for students, and Amitabha's Pure Land as the ultimate refuge. He himself kept a daily course of sixty thousand Buddha-recitations; in time he reached the state of recitation without reciting, so the sacred name was never interrupted.

In the spring of the Nham Dan year, the Master entrusted the temple to his foremost disciple, saying: "I am about to return to the West!". That winter he held a Buddha-recitation retreat. After little more than a week, in meditation he saw the water of merit glistening in the jeweled pond in splendor. Before long he felt slightly ill; he refused medicine, recited the Buddha's name with single mind, and had his disciples take turns in supporting recitation. He then gave up food and drink, lay in the auspicious posture on his right side, and maintained silent vajra recitation. The next day he saw Amitabha manifest, the white curl's light shining brilliantly; he at once rose, sat in lotus posture facing west, and told them to clear away the bedding. The attendant hesitated, objecting that the weather was too cold, but the Master said: "I am about to cast off a worn robe for a jeweled one, exchanging an illusory filthy body for a beautiful jeweled one!". When the monks heard and gathered, he calmly looked all around and slowly asked: "What is liberation?". They looked at one another, none understanding. The Master smiled and said: "In that case, better to learn from simple old country folk: keep a lifelong vegetarian diet and sincerely recite the Buddha's name — that is the surest of all!". He then had them strike the wooden bell for supporting recitation; after a moment, as the bell quickened, he bade them stop and instead chant Nam mô A Di Đà Phật in unison. After some hundred utterances, the Master joined his palms and passed away. This was the thirteenth day of the twelfth month in the twenty-eighth year of Guangxu. Some hours later the assembly found the crown of his head still warm and his body soft and supple.

The Master lived sixty-four years, with forty-four monastic years.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Layman Duong Kiet (Wuwei Zi) of the Song dynasty, who awakened at Mount Tai, turned to the Pure Land, wrote celebrated exhortations including the preface to the Ten Doubts on the Pure Land, and passed away with a verse, later seen seated upon a lotus in the West.
noi_dung:
DUONG KIET

Layman Duong Kiet, styled Thu Cong, lived under the Song, in Wuwei county, and so called himself theinactive One. In the Yuanfeng years he served as Minister of Rites. At first he favored Zen, regularly attending the Dharma assemblies of Zen Master Thien Y Hoai and investigating the sayings of Layman Pang. When by imperial command he went to offer sacrifice on the summit of Mount Tai and saw the red sun rise like a blazing round tray, he suddenly attained great awakening.

At the end of the Xining years, while mourning his mother at home, he read through the canon in his leisure and turned toward the Pure Land. He had an image of Amitabha painted, one zhang and six tall, which he carried with him for contemplation. His writings in life mostly pointed toward the Land of Bliss. He once wrote a preface to Master Tiantai's Ten Doubts on the Pure Land as follows:

"If the love of this world does not weigh heavily, one is not born in the Saha world. If Buddha-recitation is not single-minded, one is certainly not reborn in the Land of Bliss. The Saha is a defiled evil land; the Land of Bliss is a fair and pure realm. Life in the Saha is limited; the lifespan in the Land of Bliss is endless! In the Saha there are abundant sufferings and little joy. In the Land of Bliss affliction and suffering are gone and peace is immeasurable. — In the Saha one revolves with karma, never knowing when liberation will come. In the Land of Bliss, once reborn, one never retrogresses and advances step by step to the fruit of great awakening. If one wishes to deliver beings in the ten directions, one goes freely at will, no longer bound by karma. Comparing the two lands — defiled and evil versus fair and pure, affliction and suffering versus peace and joy, brief life versus long lifespan, endless wandering versus swift realization — they are opposites in every way. And yet sentient beings in their delusion do not know it. Is that not deeply pitiable?"

Amitabha is the one who gathers and escorts beings in the Land of Bliss. Shakyamuni Buddha is the guide to the Pure Land in the Saha world. Hence in his Mahayana teachings he again and again earnestly exhorts beings to rebirth there. The bodhisattvas Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta assist Amitabha, riding together the boat of the great vow into the sea of rebirth, abiding neither on this shore nor the other nor midstream, working at deliverance. Thus the Amitabha Sutra says: 'If a good man or good woman, hearing of Amitabha Buddha, holds fast his name, whether for one day up to seven days, with single undistracted mind — when life ends, Amitabha Buddha with the host of holy ones will appear before that person. At life's end, the mind free from distortion, that person will at once be reborn in Amitabha Buddha's Land of Bliss!' Thus in former days at the Hall of Impermanence in Jetavana, the Buddha taught the sick to lie facing west and contemplate rebirth in the Pure Land. Why? Because Amitabha emits light illumining the whole Dharma-realm, gathering in Buddha-reciting beings without exception. Since sage and ordinary share one mind-essence, the responsive communion accords: where there is recitation, there is response. Thus sentient beings within the Buddhas' minds, if they turn back, find every thought a Pure Land. The Buddhas within sentient beings' minds shine their sacred light everywhere; every place is compassion.

Judging by this: the wise are easily reborn, for they cut off doubt. The meditative are easily reborn, for their minds are unscattered. Precept-keepers are easily reborn, for they are far from defilement. The generous are easily reborn, for they cast off worldly goods. The patient are easily reborn, for they harbor no resentment. The diligent are easily reborn, for pure mindfulness swiftly matures. Those who have done neither good nor evil are also easily reborn, for their whole heart turns in single refuge. Those who have done evil, whose karmic retribution has already appeared, are also easily reborn, if they know shame and fear and recite the Buddha's name. On the contrary, those who have performed many wholesome meritorious deeds, if they lack faith, vows, and dedication, will surely not attain rebirth!

Oh! Amitabha's name is so easy to recite, the Pure Land so easy to be born into! Beings who will not recite and will not seek rebirth leave the Buddha, for all his pity, no means to help them. Moreover: creating evil karma one falls into painful destinies; reciting Amitabha one is born into a joyful land — both are the Buddha's words. Beings fear only falling into hell, yet doubt rebirth — is that not delusion too?

In the Yuanyou years he served as Judicial Commissioner of the Two Zhe regions, and died in office. At the end, he spoke this verse:

In life, nothing to cling to;

In death, nothing to cast away.

Between the vast void,

Let be whatever may!

Bring delusion to deliverance,

O Western Land of Bliss!

Earlier, the Right Counselor Vuong Trong Hoi, his neighbor, had studied Buddha-recitation under Thu Cong and asked: "How may it become uninterrupted?". He answered: "Once faith is certain and doubt is gone, it is uninterrupted!". Trong Hoi understood, departed joyfully, and returned home. The next year, when Thu Cong served at Don Duong, one night he dreamed that Trong Hoi came and said: "Thanks to your instruction on the Pure Land, I have now attained rebirth, and have come to thank you!". Having spoken, he bowed and withdrew. A few days later the layman received the funeral notice from Vuong Trong Hoi's son, recounting how his father had foreknown his rebirth and gone about bidding farewell to relatives and friends. After Thu Cong himself had passed away, Lady Kinh Duong dreamed she wandered to the Western Land and saw one of dignified bearing seated upon a lotus, wearing a jeweled cap and jeweled necklaces, his robe fluttering lightly in the breeze. Asked who it was, she was told it was the Inactive One, Duong Kiet.

—oOo—

Part 2

tom_tat: Layman Vuong Co of the Song dynasty, whose family kept the precept against killing for seven generations, who propagated Buddha-recitation in writings such as the Direct Pointers, and was later seen seated upon a lotus in the Pure Land together with Cat Phien.
noi_dung:
VUONG CO

Layman Vuong Co, styled Man Trong, lived under the Song at the Eastern Capital. He was the great-great-grandson of the statesman Vuong Van Dang. For seven generations his family had kept the precept against killing, and in his turn the layman vowed to release one million living beings.

While serving in Jiangxi, he studied Zen together with elder masters such as Hoi Duong and Duong Ky. He authored the Direct Pointers Resolving Doubts on the Pure Land, spreading Buddha-recitation. In leisure his rosary never left his hand; walking, standing, sitting, or lying, he cultivated pure contemplation without rest. He wrote a preface to the Precious Pearl Collection on the Pure Land as follows:

"When beings' minds are pure, the Buddha-land is pure; the Dharma-nature is unborn yet ever being born. Now there is a World Honored One dwelling in the Land of Bliss. That Buddha is now expounding the Dharma, named Amitabha. In that land, conditions are excellent and beautiful, the lifespan long. Its transforming lord's compassion and vows are vast and deep, receiving all kinds. The Buddha's light is boundless, gathering in all conscious beings of the ten directions. The scenery is wondrously fair and pure, adorned beyond conception! Jeweled nets stretch bright across the sky; jeweled trees stand in rows upon the ground. Pond waters hold the eight virtues; jade lotuses emit myriad colors. Six times daily one hears heavenly music, clear and lingering; a hundred million lands scatter wondrous flowers in offering. The Buddhas of the six directions join in praise; beings of the ten quarters take refuge in recitation and vows. The conscious within the mind are immeasurable; thought after thought they are reborn. Amitabha within beings' minds ever gathers and transforms. Entrusting one's substance to the lotus, one never leaves this very place. Roaming spiritually in the pure land, one never goes outside one's own mind. Like a mirror holding myriad images, with no coming or going; like the moon hidden in a thousand rivers, neither rising nor setting! The Dharma-gate is perfect and sudden, and all are of the rank of one more birth as successor Buddhas. The door opens to the provisional vehicle, arraying the nine grades of lotus. Reciting Immeasurable Light within one's nature — from the first there is no reciting. Born into the Land of Nurturing of the mind-only — fundamentally there is no birth. Escaping delusion and suffering, ten recitations carry one beyond to the Lotus Pond. Returning to the realm of suchness, the three vehicles together realize the fruit of wondrous awakening. A great stone, carried across, need not sink. A light boat with the current meets no obstruction. In delusion the road, though near, is far. In awakening the path is never distant.

Alas! Those of little learning and many hindrances, deep doubt and shallow wisdom, who denounce Buddha-recitation as a lesser provisional gate, or who are deluded about whether the Pure Land exists or not — do they know that to scorn Buddha-recitation is to scorn the patriarchs Yongming and Zhiyi, and to deny the Pure Land is to deny the great beings Nagarjuna and Ashvaghosa? Such persons neither believe they themselves will receive the prophecy of enlightenment nor consent to return to the homeland of original awakening. And so, caged birds and netted fish, they still sport heedlessly; in a life of wind-blown torch and fleeting shadow, they mistake a dream for permanence. When the retribution body ends, where are life's pleasures? Revolving endlessly, they vainly enter the destinies of suffering! Never thinking: the Awakened Lord exhorts us, his golden mouth never ceasing. So that one may gain holy companions in an instant and perfect marks in a moment. First receiving bliss far from the five defilements, then with increased compassion rescuing beings from the three lower paths. To neglect this is truly pitiable!".

Under Emperor Huizong, he served as Vice Minister of Revenue, was slandered and dismissed, and thereupon recited the Buddha's name and passed away. A monk whose spirit roamed the Pure Land saw Vuong Co seated upon a lotus together with Cat Phien. Cat Phien, a native of Chengjiang, rose to the office of Grand Master for Court Discussion. Whether at his office or at home, he kept a separate pure room for venerating the Buddha. One day
during worship, relics fell from the sky. Later, without illness, he sat upright facing west, recited the Buddha's name, and passed away.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Layman Ngu Thuan Hy, who recited the Buddha's name from the age of three, awakened through Zen, was guided by Master Van The to the Pure Land, and retired with his brother to devote their remaining years wholly to Buddha-recitation.
noi_dung:
NGU THUAN HY

Layman Ngu Thuan Hy, styled Truong Nhu, was a native of Qiantang. At birth he lay on his back, alert, without closing his eyes. At three years old his mouth recited the Buddha's name unceasingly, and he often saw lotus blossoms and jeweled trees appear in the house. When Thuan Hy described these visions, his grandmother said: "Those are auspicious signs of the West!", and thereupon taught him to practice meditation. From then on he would often sit upright in lotus posture with lowered eyelids. His younger brother Thuan Trinh, styled Tang Nhu, also had wholesome Buddhist roots, and in youth the two were deeply intimate. While mourning their mother, both cultivated the Tiantai practice of calming and insight.

Grown up, Thuan Hy worked as a village tutor, often instructing his pupils in the gate of contemplation. This displeased his landlord, but he paid it little mind. He then passed the provincial examination and moved to Bi Mountain to teach. He once joined a society of friends in reciting the Liang Emperor Repentance, whereupon auspicious clouds gathered in the house, strange light shone into the chamber, sweet dew fell wetting the walls, and rain brought forth yellow rice, black glutinous grain, aloeswood, and incense. Though it was midwinter, a hundred flowers bloomed all around. Moved by these miraculous signs, Thuan Hy's meditative power grew firmer, so that he could foretell events. When Great Master Van The heard of this, he cautioned: "These are only passing wholesome visions. If you take them for realization, you will surely fall into Mara's net!".

In the eleventh year of Wanli under the Ming, he passed the metropolitan examination, but owing to his father's death returned home to keep vigil in a hut beside the grave for three years. In his leisure he received the refuge precepts from Master Van The. Dwelling in the grave-hut near the mountains, each day he offered rice to the deer and hares, shouting to drive away any tigers or leopards that came. When mourning was fulfilled, he took office as a secretary in the Ministry of Justice. Before long he resigned again and climbed Mount Tianmu, sitting before the coffin-stupa of the ancient Zen Master Gaofeng Miao, practicing Zen day and night. On the twenty-first day, weary in body and about to rest awhile, he dreamed as it were that Zen Master Gaofeng Miao severed his left arm — and suddenly, vastly awakened. He brought this state to Master Van The for confirmation. The Master said: "When one newly wakes, if instead of rising to wash and bind one's kerchief one still lies easy among quilts and pillows, one will surely fall back into dreams. So it is with one newly awakened to the Way: without adorning oneself with effort, but lingering amid defilement, one will surely grow deluded again. Young bamboo breaks easily; lotuses near fire soon wither. You must take care of yourself, and not let one small glimmer hinder your further progress!". Thereupon the Master urged the layman to recite the Buddha's name and dedicate the merit toward the Pure Land, continuing the wholesome causes of former lives. Thuan Hy bowed in thanks and vowed lifelong observance.

A visitor came who said he did not believe in Buddha-recitation. The layman said: "To awaken oneself and awaken others, with the conduct of awakening complete — that is called Buddha. Reciting the Buddha is reciting awakening. In every thought to be unawakened rather than ever awakened — can that be right? Birds roost on mounds and tall trees; people dwell in hamlets, lands, and countries. Not to settle in wholesome ground but in unwholesome ground — can that be right? Reciting the Buddha and seeking the Land of Bliss is precisely going toward awakening and being born in wholesome ground, to safeguard that awakening!". The man seemed to wake as from sleep, bowed gratefully, and asked how to recite the Buddha's name. The layman answered: "In each utterance of the sacred name, arouse right mindfulness, and simply continue thus. For a hundred thousand skillful means lie in the single word 'awakening.' If one keeps every thought upon Amitabha — Immeasurable Life, Immeasurable Light — how could one fail to enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision? Students of the Way seek precisely to escape the round of birth and death. Keeping every thought thus, how could one fail to escape?

Before long he was recalled to serve as vice director in the Ministry of Rites, then promoted to director of honors. But after a while he again retired, and with his brother Thuan Trinh lived in seclusion, nourishing their nature and roaming among mountains and waters. At that time Master Van The was lecturing on the Complete Enlightenment Sutra at Nanping. The Master founded a Life-Release Society, raising funds to dig the Pond of Ten Thousand Works. Monastics and laity numbering in the tens of thousands gathered in support, and the sound of sutra chanting and Buddha-recitation shook mountains and forests. The brothers Thuan Hy rendered great service in leading many Confucian scholars and gentlemen to join that assembly. When the work was complete, three release ponds with dikes had been dug and many pavilions built for freeing birds and fish.

When all was finished, Thuan Hy withdrew into the mountains of Nanping, while Thuan Trinh secluded himself on Vulture Mountain. The two brothers resolved to spend their remaining years devoted to Buddha-recitation, to accomplish rebirth and appear no more.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Layman Vien Hoang Dao of the Ming dynasty, author of the Joint Treatise on the West, who with his brothers turned from Zen to the Pure Land, and whose younger brother Trung Dao (Tieu Tu) journeyed in spirit to the Pure Land and recorded the celebrated Journey to the Pure Land, with the rebirth of the boy Vien Dang.
noi_dung:
VIEN HOANG DAO

Vien Hoang Dao, styled Trung Lang, known as Layman Thach Dau, was a native of Gongan county, Hubei. His elder brother Tong Dao, styled Ba Tu, was known as Layman Huong Quang; his younger brother Trung Dao, styled Tieu Tu, was known as Layman Thuong Sanh. The three brothers, born of one mother, were famed in youth for literary talent, and grown up all delighted in Zen. Under the Ming, in the Wanli years, all three successively passed the metropolitan examinations. Ba Tu rose to Right Expositor-in-waiting; Tieu Tu rose to director in the Ministry of Rites. Later both brothers retired to their homeland, diligently worshipping morning and evening.

As for Trung Lang, that is Hoang Dao: after passing the examination he was appointed magistrate of Wujiang, where he judged lawsuits with great clarity and dispatch. When free from office he delighted in roaming among mountains and waters, and was later promoted to secretary in the Ministry of Rites before resigning on grounds of illness. The layman laid out a garden south of the city walls, planting ten thousand green willows. When the wind blew, standing on the high tower one saw the willow tips bend like a thousand waves, while orioles and other birds vied in song within. He called the scene "Willow Waves and Oriole Rivalry," and often roamed there with literati and Zen guests, sometimes drinking wine and chanting poems, sometimes discussing the Way. At first he studied Zen under Ly Trac Ngo, his understanding penetrating, his eloquence unhindered. But examining himself, he found that however far his subtle disquisitions ranged, they were only empty words of no real benefit, and so he turned toward the Pure Land, repenting and reciting morning and evening, and keeping the precepts. Ba Tu and Tieu Tu likewise resolved to recite the Buddha's name. The layman selected from the sutras and teachings and composed the Joint Treatise on the West. In it he discussed nature and characteristics to the point of perfect interfusion, entering deeply into the gate of nonduality. A few essential passages are briefly excerpted here: "Among the five kinds of practices, the first is the practice of faith. The sutra says: 'Faith is the first step into the Way, the mother of meritorious virtues.' Thus faith is the true cause of all practices. Even the perfect fulfillment of bodhi merely completes this root of faith — like a young bamboo shoot growing into a towering stalk, first and last a single root. No newly aspiration bodhisattva fails to succeed through the power of faith. In the Lotus school, faith is the very root. Then how should one believe?

First, believe that the fundamental wisdom and unmoving wisdom of Amitabha Buddha are not different from one's own. Like vast space: when the sun shines it is bright, when clouds gather it is dark, yet space itself has no nature of brightness or darkness. Understand, too, that sun and clouds lie nothing apart from the essence of space.

Second, believe that the practices Amitabha cultivated through countless kalpas, doing what is hard to do and enduring what is hard to endure, you too can do. Why? Because in countless past kalpas, while sunk in the three evil destinies, enduring immeasurable suffering of body and mind — sometimes wearing fur and horns, sometimes fallen amid boiling cauldrons and burning beds — such fruitless sufferings you have already undergone and endured; how much more, then, can you perform the bodhisattva's myriad practices for self and others?

Third, believe that Amitabha's immeasurable wisdom, spiritual powers, and fulfillment of immeasurable vows and works, you too shall attain. For within the Thus Come One's means of self-nature lie such inconceivable works in full. And because you and the Thus Come One share one and the same pure self-nature.

Fourth, believe that Amitabha neither comes nor goes, and you too neither come nor go; the Land of Bliss and the Saha are not separated by a hair's tip — wish to see, and you see. Why? Because both lands dwell within one undifferentiated true mind, here or there undivided. And because all Buddhas take the Dharma-nature as body and land.

Fifth, believe that Amitabha, practicing through immeasurable boundless kalpas until attaining the Way, never departs a single instant, and you too, without departing a single instant, stand level with the Buddhas. Why? Because time is illusory and unreal, gathered into falsely discriminating karma. Within the ocean of the Dharma-realm, the reality of karma cannot be found. To believe and understand thus is to enter the Way with a believing mind; it is the Pure Land faith-practice of all Buddhas.

Third is the practice of the six perfections. The Awakening of Faith Treatise says: 'The bodhisattva deeply understands that present practice is fundamentally apart from marks. Knowing the essence of the true mind is apart from greed and stinginess, he accordingly practices the perfection of giving. Knowing the essence of the true mind is undefiled, apart from the faults of the five desires, he accordingly practices the perfection of precept-keeping. Knowing the essence of the true mind has no marks of body and mind, apart from laziness, he accordingly practices the perfection of diligence. Knowing the essence of the true mind is tranquil, un рассеян, he accordingly practices the perfection of meditation. Knowing the essence of the true mind is luminous, apart from ignorance, he accordingly practices the perfection of wisdom.' Pure Land practitioners, in a single Buddha-recitation, fulfill all six gates. Thought after thought casting off is giving. Thought after thought pure is precept-keeping. Thought after thought continuing unbroken is diligence. Thought after thought gathered into oneness is meditation. Thought after thought luminous is wisdom. These six practices all flow from Buddha-recitation; principal and auxiliary are not two, phenomenon and principle are not different. Thus Buddha-recitation embraces all practices, for it is the One-Mind gate, and apart from mind there are no practices. To abandon the practices is to abandon mind; to abandon phenomena can never establish principle.'

Before long, Hoang Dao was recalled to his former post and gradually promoted to director of the honors bureau. Shortly after he again resigned on grounds of illness, returned home, and after a few days lodged at a monastery in Jingzhou city, where he devoted himself to recitation and passed away without illness.

Trung Dao, that is Tieu Tu: after retiring, morning and evening he diligently recited the Buddha's name. One night, the full moon of the tenth month in the Jiayin year, the forty-second year of Wanli, when his recitation was finished, he sat quietly and felt body and spirit lucid and clear. Suddenly, as though entering samadhi, his spirit rose above the house and, riding the clouds, flew away. On either side two youths supported him, saying: "Follow us!". They led him westward, swift as birds. Looking about, the moonlight shone clear, the lunar disk plain in the sky. Gazing below, mountains, lakes, fields, cities, and villages appeared tiny as mounds of earth, cups of water, swarms of bees, nests of ants. Sinking a little lower, he smelled a foul stench rising from below, and strove upward to the heights before he felt light and pure. Faster and faster, swift as lightning, they traveled; after a while the two youths cried: "Halt!", and together descended to the ground.

Tieu Tu looked about: the road ran straight as a stretched cord, the ground level, bright, moist, and lustrous, not of sand or stone. Along the road lay ponds more than ten fathoms wide, their steps of jeweled stone veined as if carved. In the ponds, five-colored lotuses bloomed in rivalry, of extraordinary fragrance and beauty. Along the banks stood rows of radiant trees, where strange birds sang together in harmony. At intervals golden bridges spanned the ponds as boundaries, their rails continuous as city walls. Beyond the trees on the far bank stood exquisite pavilions beyond compare. The people in the pavilions, pure and radiant as celestials, gazed at Tieu Tu and smiled. The two youths walked swiftly; the layman could not keep pace and called out: "Please wait a moment upon the bridge for me!". The youths consented, and he caught up with them and leaned together upon the bridge's jeweled rail to rest. Tieu Tu folded his hands and asked: "May I know who you are, and what place this is?". One youth answered: "We are attendants of Master Linh Hoa, who wishes to meet you and speak a little, and sent us to receive you.". The layman asked: "What manner of person is the Master?". The answer: "He is your elder brother, Vien Hoang Dao, styled Trung Lang. When you meet you will know; now we must hasten on!". Having spoken, they crossed the bridge and followed the road to a grove of more than a thousand great trees with emerald leaves and golden-petaled blossoms. Beyond the grove lay a great pond; crossing its bridge stood a gate of white jade, which one youth pushed open and entered first. The other led Tieu Tu through more than twenty tiers of pavilions, their golden hues dazzling, wondrous grasses and numinous flowers waving beside the steps. Arriving beneath a certain tower, a figure resembling Trung Lang, face bright as jade, robes like sunset clouds, over a fathom tall, came forward to welcome him, joyfully saying: "So you have come, brother!", and led him by the hand up the tower, where four or five figures like celestials sat around. Trung Lang said: "This is the borderland of the West. Practitioners of Buddha-recitation whose faith and understanding are immature and whose jewel of precepts is incomplete are mostly born here. ...

Beings of the ten directions who are reborn entrust their substance to those lotus blossoms; when the flower duly opens, they go each to his pavilion and gather with fellow pure practitioners of affinity. Since there are no beauties or alluring sounds, superior understanding is easily accomplished, and before long they advance to birth in the true land of the Land of Bliss! Tieu Tu thought to himself: 'A scene so beautiful, and yet still the borderland?' He asked: "Where have you been born, brother?". Trung Lang answered: "My pure vows were earnest, but defiled emotion was not yet extinct; at first I was born here for a while, but now I have reached the Pure Land. Yet because my understanding exceeded my precepts, I belong only to the earth-dwelling rank and may not dwell with the great bodhisattvas in the pavilions amid the sky; I must advance further. Fortunately, while in the Saha, thanks to sharp wisdom I composed the Joint Treatise on the West praising the Thus Come One's inconceivable merit in delivering beings, and so I have the reward of flying freely, roaming through Buddha-lands. Wherever the Buddhas preach the Dharma, I may go to hear — a truly excellent thing!"

Having spoken, he took Tieu Tu's hand and flew up into the sky, crossing a thousand myriad leagues in an instant, then alighted somewhere. Here there was no day or night, no sun or moon; the radiance was brilliant and unobstructed. The ground of lapis lazuli shone clear within and without; pillars and cords of gold and the seven treasures intersected, marking boundaries. The trees were all of sandalwood and auspicious kinds, row upon row facing one another, in tens of thousands of tiers. From every leaf sprang beautiful blossoms of wondrous hues and rare treasures. Beneath the trees lay jeweled ponds, their countless gentle waves spontaneously sounding the wondrous Dharma. The pond bottoms were laid purely with diamond sand. Within the ponds, precious lotuses of myriad colors emitted rays of varied hues. Along the rows of trees by the ponds, majestic pavilions wound in and out of sight, eaves jutting, pillars upholding curving roofs, great doors and latticed windows shedding light upon one another, great jeweled curtains hanging all about — every adornment complete. Around the pavilions hung countless musical instruments that sounded of themselves, performing the sounds of the Dharma. What is recorded in the Amitabha and Immeasurable Life sutras, compared with this, does not reach even one part in ten. Looking up, many pavilions floated amid the sky, wondrously fair among banks of sunset clouds. Trung Lang said: "What you see is the scene of earth-dwelling beings in the Pure Land. Beyond this lies the abode of the Dharma-body great bodhisattvas, whose scenery is a thousand myriad times more beautiful, and whose spiritual powers a thousand myriad times greater. By wisdom-power I may visit, but may not dwell there. Beyond that is the abode of the tenth-ground and equal-enlightenment bodhisattvas, which I cannot reach nor comprehend. Farther still is the realm of wondrous enlightenment, which only Buddha together with Buddha can behold!".

Having spoken, they flew together to another place, where the halls blazed with extraordinary light, of unknown substance. Beside this treasure, yellow gold and white jade seemed earthen in hue. Here there were no city walls, only encircling rails. The two sat together beneath a pavilion and conversed. Trung Lang said: "I never imagined such perfect beauty and joy! If while in the Saha I had kept the precepts more strictly, my bliss would not be only this! In general: first, when understanding exceeds precepts, the grade of birth is very high. Next, when precepts and understanding are equal, the birth is very secure. (Exceeding understanding: profound liberating insight. Equal precepts: strict keeping of the precepts.) If there is understanding without precepts, most are dragged by karma into birth among the eight classes of gods and ghosts. Fellow practitioners fallen into that state I have seen a great many; as for you, brother, your prajna disposition is deep but your power of precepts and meditation is weak. To awaken to the subtle truth without giving rise to precepts and meditation is mere mad wisdom! When you return to the Saha, while still strong you must truly awaken and truly practice, keep pure vows earnest, diligently practice skillful means to help others, pity all beings — and before long we shall meet again. If heedless and fallen into other paths, it will be truly dreadful! If you cannot yet keep the precepts fully, follow Master Nagarjuna's six fasting days. Among the precepts, the killing precept is most weighty. Convey my message to fellow practitioners: no one who daily wields the knife to kill, mouth greedy for fine flavors, has ever been reborn in the Land of Bliss! Though one may preach like raining flowers and rolling clouds, without true practice in earnest cultivation, it is all in vain! You and I, since the time of King Emptiness Buddha, have through many lives been brothers, and through our wandering in the six destinies ever so! Now by good fortune I have reached an excellent place; fearing you may fall into evil destinies, I have used spiritual powers and skillful means to bring you here and exhort you. Now the karmic conditions of the two realms, pure and defiled, differ, and you cannot stay long!".

Tieu Tu hastened to ask about the rebirth of Ba Tu and of departed fellow practitioners. Trung Lang answered: "The births of our brother Tong Dao and the others are all excellent; hereafter you will know of yourself!". Having spoken, he rose into the sky and flew away. Tieu Tu stood and strolled slowly along the pond bank enjoying the scene, when suddenly, as if slipping, he plunged into the water — and woke with a start. His whole body was bathed in sweat; turning, he saw the spent lamp still upon its stand, the bright moonlight still shining through the window — the fourth watch had already begun. He at once took brush and paper and recorded this "Journey to the Pure Land."

Earlier, Tong Dao had a son named Vien Dang, only thirteen, who fell mortally ill with congestion. The boy said to Hoang Dao: "I am about to die; uncle, how can you save me?". Trung Lang said: "Simply devote yourself to Buddha-recitation and you will surely be reborn in the Land of Bliss. This defiled land is not worth clinging to!". The boy at once joined his palms and recited Nam mô A Di Đà Phật without pause, while the family joined in support. After a moment he smiled and said: "I see a lotus, slightly red in hue.". Reciting a little longer, he said: "The flower grows steadily larger, fresh and bright in color, indescribably beautiful!". In a moment he said again: "The Buddha has come, of excellent marks and radiance, his tall body filling the whole house!". Presently his breathing grew labored. Tong Dao said: "Let the family support you; you need only utter the single word 'Buddha' at the very end.". Vien Dang uttered "Buddha" a few times, joined his palms, and passed away.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Layman Vuong Dien of the Song dynasty, author of the Record of the Self-Nature of the Pure Land, who explained how the Pure Land carries ordinary beings directly to non-retrogression, and passed away facing west amid strange fragrance, leaving over a hundred relics.
noi_dung:
VUONG DIEN

Layman Vuong Dien, styled Vo Cong, lived under the Song, a native of Cixi county in Mingzhou. He was very intelligent and deeply learned, but twice failed the metropolitan examinations. From then on his ambition for fame faded like cold ashes; he ate vegetarian food, wore coarse cloth, and attended every sutra lecture. In old age he devoted himself to the Buddha-Recitation samadhi and authored the Record of the Self-Nature of the Pure Land, writing his own preface:

"The special wonder of the Pure Land gate taught by the World Honored One can be summed in a single phrase: 'It carries beings from the rank of ordinary persons directly across to the stage of non-retrogression!' Why? — In this world, when a practitioner realizes the First Faith of the Perfect Teaching or the First Fruit of the Lesser Vehicle, wrong views and the three poisons never again arise. That is the realm of severing delusion and awakening (karmic delusion extinguished, awakening arisen), directly entering the stream of sages: though passing through rebirth, one never loses what has been realized. That rank transcends the four evil destinies (hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras) and never loses a heavenly or human body. But all ordinary persons, even bodhisattvas of the initial resolve who have reached the stage of subduing delusion and awakening (delusion sunk into the store-consciousness, awakening arisen), once they pass through the extraordinary transformation of birth and death, at once forget what they realized and practiced. Hence such persons, meeting adverse conditions, may retrogress and fall into the three lower paths.

But in the Land of Common Residence of sages and ordinary beings in the Land of Bliss, though it too holds the tiers of the three realms, there are only humans and celestials. Thus all conscious beings born there are forever done with the four destinies and freed from rebirth. With supporting conditions complete and lifespan endless, even the dullest, in one lifetime of practice, all realize sagehood. How then could there be retrogression? The Buddhas' intent in urging and praising is nothing beyond this. If the superior capacity resolves upon Buddha-recitation, that is the supreme pure karma and will join a high grade. As for the most ignorant rustics, if they sincerely recite the Buddha's name and vow rebirth, none will fail to attain it.

Alas! Reflecting upon the Pure Land gate, one knows the Buddha abandons not a single being! Those who cling to emptiness in folly, imitate unobstructed conduct, then in pride seek to cut off others' Buddha-recitation — are they not deeply pitiable?".

Early on the night of the Dinh Mao day in the leap month of the sixteenth year of Shaoxing, strange fragrance suddenly filled the house. The layman said to his Dharma student, the monk Tu Te: "This is evoked by this old man's pure karma!". Having spoken, he bathed, changed his robes, sat upright facing west, joined his palms, and attained rebirth. At the cremation, one hundred and eight rice-grain relics were recovered.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Layman Vuong Nhut Huu (Longshu) of the Song dynasty, author of the widely circulated Longshu Pure Land Writings, who stood upright at his passing; Layman Vien Liet Tinh, who defended the Pure Land gate; and Lady Viet Quoc, who through a dream journey beheld the lotus pond where each reciter's flower blooms or withers with diligence or sloth.
noi_dung:
VUONG NHUT HUU

Layman Vuong Nhut Huu, styled Hu Trung, was a native of Luzhou. Under Emperor Gaozong of the Song, he passed the national doctoral examination, but declined office and retired to his homeland to teach. He then gave up teaching as well, kept a lifelong vegetarian diet, wore coarse cloth, and cultivated the pure karma with single purpose. Each day he bowed one thousand prostrations to the Buddha and then recited the sacred name. He authored the Longshu Pure Land Writings, widely circulated in his time. In it the language is simple, with many parables, urging everyone from princes, officials, and scholars down to commoners, butchers, servants, and singers to take refuge and recite the Buddha's name. His arguments are lucid, his intent utterly sincere, moving many to be transformed and practice.

In the Gui Si year of the Qiandao era, Mr. Ly Ngan Bac of Luling fell gravely ill and dreamed of one who called himself Layman Longshu, saying: "When you wake, take plain rice gruel and you will recover. Do you remember a good friend, Khuyet Trong Nha, who urged you to the direct path?". Ngan Bac replied: "I have followed his counsel and recite the Buddha's name daily!". Upon waking, he had plain gruel cooked and eaten, and indeed the illness eased. Ngan Bac then sent his sons to find Vuong Nhut Huu and receive instruction. Before long the sons returned and reported: "Layman Longshu has already been reborn in the Buddha-land. Three days before his passing, he went about bidding farewell to relatives and friends, urging them to practice diligently, saying he was about to journey far and they would meet no more. On the final day he gathered his old disciples, instructed them, and performed his recitation as usual. At the third watch, he suddenly chanted the Buddha's name aloud a few times and said: 'Amitabha has come to escort me!' Then, standing upright, he passed away...". Seeing the portrait of Vuong Nhut Huu which his sons had borrowed and brought home — exactly the person he had met in his dream — Ly Ngan Bac was deeply moved, had an image of Layman Longshu carved, and spread the story far and wide. From then on, devotees throughout Luling resolved to recite the Buddha's name.

In the Xianchun years, Mr. Lu Nguyen Ich re-carved the Longshu Pure Land Writings. When the carving reached the chapter of dedication, three relics suddenly appeared upon the block. His uncle Ly Su Thuyet recorded the event at the head of that chapter.

—oOo—

VIEN LIET TINH

Vien Liet Tinh, a native of Kunshan, often lodged in the Xikou region of Hangzhou, and so called himself Layman Tay Khe. As a boy he studied for the examinations; one day, hearing his grandmother recite the Diamond Sutra as far as "no marks of self," he found an entrance.

Later the layman met Zen Master Duyet Son and diligently investigated the upward path day by day.
