Just then Old Man Bach Tung came from Xuefeng to Kunshan; after two or three encounters, Liet Tinh penetrated his original nature and received the mind-seal. From then on his style grew daily more flourishing; teaching according to capacity with unhindered eloquence, he promoted the One Vehicle while also spreading the Pure Land. Seeing his companions fond of dry Zen or delighting in arts of immortality, mostly disbelieving the Pure Land, he wrote these words of explanation:

"The Pure Land gate is perfectly interfused and vast. Until now I have secretly practiced and silently realized it, but dared not hastily speak of it to others. That is because the season had not come, and speech would have been fruitless — not because I deliberately hid my practice.

For Buddha-recitation is the Buddhas' most profound Dharma-treasury: even among voice-hearers and solitary Buddhas of the Two Vehicles there are those who do not believe. For those venerables, abiding in the pure Nirvana state with realized spiritual powers, see and know only within a single great chiliocosm, and do not perceive the ocean of majestic Pure Land adornments established throughout the ten directions. Hence the Buddhas have rebuked clinging to the Two Vehicles' state as deviant, as falling into the pit of inaction, as drunken on the wine of samadhi! How lamentable are Zen students of today, who have not yet reached even the pure Nirvana state of the Two Vehicles, yet with empty bellies and lofty hearts claim attainment without attaining, realization without realizing. Sitting quietly until the six senses momentarily stir no more, a glimpse of scenery appears, and at once they suppose themselves awakened. Strutting ever after, they disparage the Pure Land — truly pitiable!

Even supposing they had truly and greatly awakened and touched the tip of the nose of the mother of original nature, could they stand outside the four Pure Lands, from the Land of Common Residence to the Land of Everlasting Quiescent Light? If they argue: 'Though knowing those four lands, I cast them aside!' Do they not recall the venerable Zen Master Mat Van's words: 'You wish to cast it aside — truly a case of telling dreams before the deluded!' The ancients said: 'Zen students of today take penetrating the Dharma-body as essential, yet know not what to do after penetrating. If after penetrating there remains the shadow of anything, that too is sickness!' In short, Zen students of today rarely escape the subtle demon of intellectual understanding, and in turn call Pure Land practitioners ignorant — is that not error!

Moreover, throughout empty space there are ten Dharma-realms, and the Buddhas' Pure Lands are the foremost realm, to which the other nine all return. Practicing the Pure Land in the human realm is very easy, while in the hells and hungry ghost realms, pressed by suffering and ignorant of the Buddha's name, practice is hard. The Buddhas in pity ever emit pure light with spiritual power to save them, but those beings, screened by karma, cannot see. Only when karma ends and the mind opens, hearing and reciting a single Buddha-name, do the hellish and ghostly scenes at once turn cool and clear. As for animals, darkened by folly, and asuras, blazing with anger, they too can hardly behold the compassionate light. As for celestials, enjoying supreme pleasures, they likewise find Buddha-recitation hard to practice.

But examine closely: none are more resistant to Pure Land practice than the celestial immortals. It is not that they do not know the Pure Land is beautiful — but having gained spiritual powers, transformations, flight, and free appearance and disappearance in being or nonbeing, able to emit lights and conjure images of Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and adorned scenes, they suppose the joys of the Pure Land are no more than this, and will not turn toward it. They do not know they have fallen into phantasmal consciousness, and that the conjured scenes all arise from blended essence, energy, and spirit! The Buddha said: celestials who do not follow right awakening have not reached non-action; when their reward ends they fall with karma into the destinies! The true-celestial scene manifests of itself and is not forged by luyện; what is forged by luyện, being produced, cannot escape extinction. Original essence and energy lie nothing apart from original spirit, and original spirit is but another name for karmic consciousness. The great man must return to original nature, cut off spirit-consciousness, sever the root of life — why forge an original spirit within the round of karmic consciousness? Some who forge it find their powers fail midway, decaying before the kalpa-fire arrives. Even if the original spirit can be made to endure, at the great kalpa-fire not only the material body is destroyed but the immaterial body is burned as well. Do not console yourselves that your way is like space — it too is karmic consciousness in phantasmal display, which only one realized in the supreme wisdom-eye sees through. Though celestials may conjure excellent scenes, in the end they attain neither full clarity nor full rectitude. How could they compare with the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and all the principal and dependent rewards of the Pure Land dwelling together in radiance more piercing than a hundred thousand suns? Realized followers of Buddhism see time and space as illusory, and can manifest a jeweled royal land upon a hairtip and turn the Dharma-wheel within a dustmote — a state celestials cannot match in one part of myriad. Therefore whoever deeply believes the Pure Land gate and truly practices ...

The Pure Land gate is the refuge of all sages. Once reborn in the Land of Bliss, perfecting blessings and wisdom, one returns to the Saha: meeting immortals, delivering immortals; meeting humans, delivering humans; meeting demons and ghosts, delivering demons and ghosts; meeting even creditors of enmity, delivering them too. That is truly the work of the great man! If you firmly believe the Pure Land gate and resolve upon true practice, the lotus in the jeweled pond of the Land of Bliss will bloom fresh with your name. Even now, when Buddha-recitation becomes pure, all fair scenes, Dharma-sounds, wondrous fragrances, subtle lights, and true principles flood eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Then your very selves have already become ancient Buddhas!".

In the second month of the fiftieth year of Kangxi under the Qing, the layman recited the Buddha's name and peacefully attained rebirth at Baoshou, at sixty-two. His disciples gathered his remaining words into the Collected Works of Layman Tay Khe.

—oOo—

LADY VIET QUOC

Lady Viet Quoc, nee Vuong, was the wife of Prince Kinh. Prince Kinh was the uncle of Emperor Zhezong of the Song. The Lady recited the Buddha's name day and night unceasingly, and guided her maids and concubines to practice the Pure Land and seek the Land of Bliss. Among them one maid was often lazy. The Lady summoned her and said: "For one person alone you shall not ruin my rule!", and expelled her from the group.

Frightened and repentant, the maid resolved upon diligent Buddha-recitation, sparing no toil. One day she told a fellow servant: "I am about to journey far!". That night strange fragrance filled the room; without any illness she passed away. A few days later the fellow servant reported to the Lady: "Last night I dreamed the departed maid asked me to convey boundless gratitude for your grace. Thanks to your rebuke, she has been reborn in the Land of Bliss!". The Lady said: "If she can appear in my own dream, then I shall believe!". That night the Lady dreamed the departed maid came to thank her as foretold, and asked: "Can the Western Land be visited?". The maid said yes, and led the Lady flying away. In a moment they reached a vast jeweled pond, its lights blending in piercing brilliance. Within the pond, large and small lotuses of many colors and radiances intermingled, some fresh, some withered. Asked why, the maid said: "When a being in the Saha first resolves to recite the Buddha's name and seek the Land of Bliss, a lotus is conjured here. If that person practices diligently day by day, the flower grows ever larger and fresher. If midway one grows gradually lazy, the flower will wither. If practice ceases, the flower fades and vanishes. But if one earnestly recites again, another lotus springs forth. If for long one's effort never retrogresses, the pure fruit will ripen. When that person casts off the retribution body in the Saha, the spirit lodges in that lotus womb and waits until the flower opens and beholds the Buddha.". Gazing afar at a flower dais bearing one crowned with a jeweled cap, necklaced with jewels, robed and featured majestically, the Lady asked: "Who is that?". The maid said: "That is the Inactive Layman Duong Kiet, newly reborn here.". The Lady saw another in court dress seated upon a somewhat lesser lotus and asked again. The maid answered: "That is Layman Ma Vu; when his merit is complete he too shall soon be reborn here.". The Lady asked: "Where shall I be born? ...

Upon waking, the Lady remembered the dream clearly, her joy and grateful sorrow intermingled, and practiced with redoubled diligence. Past eighty, on her birthday morning, she rose early, held a small incense burner in both hands, its fragrant smoke curling, and stood solemnly facing the Avalokiteshvara Pavilion. Her maids in neat dress formed ranks and approached to offer birthday homage. But when they looked again, the Lady had already passed away.

A comment: Dharma Master An Quang said: "The workings of spirit and of good and evil karma are inconceivable! Some who create evil, while still alive in the world above, already suffer in hell with part of body and spirit. And Pure Land practitioners, though presently in the defiled land, are already partly born in the Lotus Land with part of their spirit.". The case of Ma Vu above is just so.

Women born into the Land of Bliss all turn into male bodies complete with the thirty-two excellent marks. Yet the maid appeared in female form to her companion and to Prince Kinh's Lady only as skillful manifestation, so that acquaintances might easily recognize her. Readers should understand this and not doubt.

—oOo—

Part 3

tom_tat: Layman Ma Vinh To, cured of grave illness through Buddha-recitation, who was escorted by the Three Holy Ones at his passing, then appeared in Abbot Tuong Phong's dream to repay with Dharma verses the kindness of the one who had guided him to the Pure Land.
noi_dung:
MA VINH TO

Layman Ma Vinh To, styled Tru Luong, was a native of Xiushui, Zhejiang. As a boy he showed literary talent, and at fifteen was admitted among the licentiates. His parents died early, and Vinh To served his stepmother with devoted filial care. At thirty he contracted spitting of blood. After five years the illness worsened until whatever he ate he vomited up.

A monk named Tuong Phong, an old acquaintance of Vinh To before leaving the household life, came to visit. Fresh from traveling study, his dormant wisdom had opened and his understanding was penetrating. Hearing the monk discourse, Vinh To marveled and asked for a cure. Tuong Phong answered: "Fellow practitioner's illness springs from past karma and cannot be cured by medicine. If you can cast off myriad involvements and devote yourself to Buddha-recitation, in time, as the work deepens, the ignorance and karmic hindrances of immeasurable kalpas will gradually be severed. Then even the root-illness of birth-and-death rebirth can be liberated — how much less this bodily illness to worry over!". Hearing this, Vinh To started awake, thereafter kept a vegetarian diet and cultivated the pure karma. From then on the illness gradually eased.

Before that time, Ma Vinh To had dreamed that amid the sky arose countless characters for "longevity," emitting brilliant light. Reading Buddhist books, he learned that Amitabha means Immeasurable Life, also called Immeasurable Light. Recalling the dream, he saw its fulfillment and secretly rejoiced, counting himself karmically bound to the Pure Land gate. He then read the Platform Sutra and awakened to the source of mind, redoubling his joy and grateful sorrow. Afterward Vinh To took the five precepts, daily recited the Diamond and Amitabha sutras, recited the Buddha's name thirty thousand times, and practiced pure contemplation. In leisure he invited fellow practitioners to gather at his home, organizing day-and-night Buddha-recitation.

In the fifty-sixth year of Qianlong, in the last ten days of the first month, Vinh To returned from Suzhou; just a month later he fell ill. By early third month he lay abed unable to rise, telling a close friend: "Since thirty-five I have aroused the bodhi-mind, seeking only the adornment of the Buddha-land and the benefit of beings, regarding the glories of high office as worn-out sandals. Now, though bearing a grave illness, my one joyful thought has never changed. At present I only keep right mindfulness, awaiting life's end to be born straight into the West!". A friend asked: "When you are gone, with several mouths at home,
who will support them?". The layman answered: "That belongs to each one's karmic blessings; it is beyond my bearing!". On the evening of the eighteenth he said: "Tomorrow must be a great repentance!". Next morning he struggled up, donned his robe, venerated the Buddha in repentance, sat facing west, recited the Buddha's name some hundred times, then knelt and read Master Lianchi's vow text before returning to bed. Three days later he said: "The Three Holy Ones of the West manifest before me and preach the Dharma for me. I ever dwell within piercing brilliant light!". The next day he said again: "The Bodhisattva sprinkles pure water upon my body, washing away past debts, leaving me cool — a joy beyond words!". That evening a fellow practitioner, Tram Hong Dieu, visited, asked whether he recited, and cautioned him against attachment to marks. The layman answered: "Still reciting — mind itself is Buddha; what attachment to marks!". He then gave up food, drinking only a few cups of tea daily, and two days later only pure cool water. On the twenty-ninth day of the third month, at noon, he told his family: "The Buddha has come to escort me!". Having spoken, he recited the sacred name continuously, then lay on his right side and attained rebirth, at forty-eight. Childless, he left instructions for an heir to be established.

At that time Abbot Tuong Phong was in closed retreat at Wenxing Pavilion in Suzhou, cultivating Buddha-Recitation samadhi. That winter, one night he dreamed three venerables entered his hut and sat on the southern side facing him. In the middle sat a monk, flanked by two laymen, their bearing solemn and dignified, each head encircled by a halo. Tuong Phong bowed and asked: "Where have the three venerables come from?". The one in mourning dress said: "We come from the Western Land!". The Abbot asked: "Are you from Amitabha Buddha's Land of Bliss?". The monk answered: "Yes!". Tuong Phong asked their names, but they did not answer, asking instead: "What is your Dharma name?". The Abbot answered: "This disciple's Dharma name is Dat Van.". The monk said: "Why speak falsely?". Tuong Phong said: "It is truly so, not false!". The monk asked again as before; the Abbot answered as before. The monk again said: "Still false speech!". Tuong Phong said: "This disciple speaks truly, not falsely!". The monk said: "All beings take the false for true and cling to the unreal as real, hence their rebirth. The wise know all dharmas are false and nominally designated, and revolve no more. Do not delude yourself and lose the true mind. Understand: the true mind is no-mind, true knowing is not-knowing; to have knowing is Mara. The Buddha is spiritually knowing yet unknowing; believe and accept without doubt!". At these words Tuong Phong suddenly awakened and said: "Your reverences' teaching is truly the Buddha's inconceivable Dharma! Since you come from the Land of Bliss, may I ask: have you beheld Amitabha Buddha?". The one on the left answered: "If I told you, you might not believe. You must see for yourself!". Then all three rose; each tapped Tuong Phong upon the head and spoke a verse in turn:

Strive on with diligence,

Cultivating the pure karma unremittingly.

Deep the cause, true the fruit —

Be heedful and never doubt!

All dharmas arise from mind

And return to ceasing from mind.

The true nature was ever empty;

Taking or casting off cannot be done!

You are already partly clear:

Buddha and beings share one mind,

Like the Shurangama samadhi,

Like scenes within a dream.

The verses finished, Ma Vinh To appeared in dignified demeanor and bowed to the three. All three rose into the sky and flew westward. Then music resounded through the air, and the sound of Buddha-recitation, high and low, clear and free. Vinh To bowed thrice more to Tuong Phong, saying: "Thanks to your reverence urging me to cultivate the pure karma and take refuge in the Three Jewels, I have been blessed with birth in the West, receiving great peace and benefit. Hence I begged the Bodhisattva to come and speak the wondrous Dharma, repaying your profound kindness!". Having spoken, he bowed farewell thrice more, joined his palms, recited the Buddha's name, and flew to the West. Just then the midnight bell rang, and Tuong Phong woke with a start. The Abbot at once took brush and paper and recorded the omen, calling it the Record of a Dream.

Later, Abbot Tuong Phong secluded himself at Phuoc Thanh Cloister in Lujiang. At the end he foreknew the day and hour, and passed away seated, reciting the Buddha's name.

A comment: Before, Can Duong borrowed a spirit-medium sitting to exhort his companions. Now Tru Luong repays profound kindness through a responsive dream. Who then says that birth in the Land of Nurturing leaves no tidings! Yet with those whose conditions are unripe, all cases cannot be judged alike!

—oOo—

tom_tat: Layman Ngo Doan Thang, saved from drowning through recitation, who branded his arm with the vow of western rebirth and founded great recitation societies in Hangzhou, passing away in clear mindfulness beholding countless bodhisattvas.
noi_dung:
NGO DOAN THANG

Layman Ngo Doan Thang, styled Thuong Dao, was a native of She county, Huizhou. In youth he often traveled trading about Suzhou and Hangzhou. While touring Tiger Hill temple and mountain, a monk chanced to meet him, studied his face, and said: "You too have wholesome roots, but alas, at twenty-nine you will meet drowning — what is to be done?". Frightened, Doan Thang asked for a means of rescue. The monk pondered a moment, then taught him: "From now on, refrain from killing and release living beings. Each day sincerely recite the Great Compassion Mantra and the Buddha's name, and you may yet escape!". Doan Thang believed and practiced, and often urged this upon others.

At twenty-nine, the layman took ship from Hangzhou homeward, with sixteen fellow travelers, seventeen in all. After sailing some dozens of miles, the tide suddenly came roaring, great waves rising in peril. Doan Thang recalled the monk's words and hastily joined his palms in Buddha-recitation. In a moment the boat capsized, and he and all the passengers were swept away by the waves. Amid dazed confusion, he heard a voice: "Ngo Doan Thang, for urging others to recite the Buddha's name, shall escape this calamity!". Hastily opening his eyes and looking about, he found himself lying on the shore, fishermen rousing him. Checking, hat, shoes, and baggage had all been swept away — only the eighteen-bead rosary he daily recited remained gripped in his hand. The other sixteen all sank without trace. From then on he believed all the more in the inconceivable merit of Buddha-recitation! Not returning home, he stayed and opened a physiognomy shop, using the connection to teach cause and effect and urge practice and recitation.

After the calamity, Doan Thang practiced with redoubled diligence. He branded his arm with incense, forming the four characters "Seeking Birth in the West" to declare his vow. In Hangzhou, following Patriarch Lianchi's legacy, many were devoted to Buddha-recitation, but the true practitioners were the elderly — no youths among them. Each month they gathered at a temple for recitation, calling it the Society of Old Fellows, not daring to assemble in great numbers for fear of suspicion as a heterodox political plot. Doan Thang declared boldly to all: "Buddha-recitation knows no distinction of male or female, old or young, noble or base. Buddhism is the true teaching, favored and recognized by the court — why fear?". At that time Dien Kiem Dien, a powerful official inspecting the salt tax in Hangzhou, was an old friend of the layman. Seizing the opportunity, he opened a subscription, first approaching Mr. Dien, who contributed two hundred taels of gold to lead the list. With the funds raised, the layman established an endowment whose light interest supported a recitation society at Baocheng Temple on Zi Yang Mountain, along with charitable works. On each assembly day he expounded the Buddha's teaching to the multitude, speaking of cause and effect, urging the unawakened to resolve and the resolved to practice diligently. He opened further branches at Xianlin Temple within the city and elsewhere for exhortation. Believers in recitation grew daily into the thousands. At each gathering all were solemn and reverent, never lax, noisy, or disorderly. The sixteen-foot Three Holy Ones in the Western Hall of Xianlin Temple were also erected by the society. One morning during assembled recitation, the assembly saw from the nose of the Mahasthamaprapta image a shaft of white light issue forth, circling the hall for over an hour before dissolving.

From then on, the manner of Buddha-recitation flourished in Hangzhou. Surrounding regions felt its transforming influence; old and young, men and women, rosary in hand and Buddha on lips, became commonplace, no longer strange. Doan Thang's name was known to every woman and child. At each assembly, local groups took turns inviting him to lecture. — West Lake's Lingfeng Temple, originally the site of Zen Master Phuc Ho, had long lain in ruins. In the first year of Daoguang, Doan Thang vowed its restoration, completing the work after several years. The layman passed away at sixty-six. At the end he kept right mindfulness clearly, saying: "I see countless bodhisattvas walking in meditation before me!". Then, seated upright, he quietly passed away. This was the first day of the fifth month in the ninth year of Daoguang.

A comment: Lo Khon recited to seek rebirth and was also freed from present sickness. Doan Thang recited only hoping to escape calamity, yet also received blessed signs at the end. Who then says: "The merit of Buddha-recitation benefits only after death"? See in these examples: both strove in true practice with unshaken faith. People today offer trifling effort yet crave excessive benefit, and seeing no effect declare the Buddha's teaching ineffective and abandon practice — is that not lamentable!

—oOo—

tom_tat: Layman Pham Nguyen Le (Dung Hoa) of the Qing dynasty, who abandoned immortalist practice for the Pure Land, escaped a perilous maric state through right mindfulness, aided the blind Mrs. Tram to rebirth, and passed away quietly with a warm crown after settling all his affairs.
noi_dung:
PHAM NGUYEN LE

Layman Pham Nguyen Le, styled Dung Hoa, lived under the Qing, a native of Qiantang. In youth he studied Confucianism, upright in conduct, serving his parents with great filial devotion. Once, when his father was ill, he cut flesh from his thigh, brewed it with medicine, and offered it; the illness was cured. When his mother, nee Du, fell gravely ill, he did the same once more, and she likewise improved.

Before long both parents passed away, and his wife followed soon after. Then in his prime, Nguyen Le, moved by life's impermanence, cast off worldly ties and followed a recluse to study the Way of immortals. After more than ten years, his effort showed some effect. Later, reading Master Van The's books, he received the Three Refuges and five precepts. Nguyen Le kept the precepts firmly: garments of silk or fur he would not use. Abandoning his former practice, he devoted himself to the Pure Land, cultivating the contemplative gate with special precision. Earlier, when his mother lay dying with clouded spirit, the layman had urged her to contemplate Avalokiteshvara with single mind, and she did so. A few days later she suddenly said: "The Bodhisattva has escorted Mother to a strange, wondrous, bright realm!", and passed away joyfully. For this reason Nguyen Le greatly rejoiced in the efficacy of contemplation.

Gentle by nature, the layman delighted in releasing life, giving alms, and aiding the poor, sick, and afflicted. In charitable works he was diligent and thorough, sparing no toil. Meeting monks and nuns, he offered support according to his means, omitting none. Thus in his time, hearing Nguyen Le's name, monastics and laity alike knew and esteemed him.

In the summer of the eighth year of Daoguang, the layman sealed himself in retreat at Dai Dong Pavilion south of the city, fixing a hundred-day term of Buddha-recitation. One day in quiet sitting, the mysterious powers of his former immortal practice suddenly manifested. He felt the pure energies of heaven and earth gather from midair in many streams, entering through crown, nose, and mouth straight down to the elixir field, merging with his own original energy. Body and mind were then most peaceful, light, and blissful beyond compare. In a moment an infant some inches tall emerged from the crown gate, flew sporting about for a time, then re-entered through the crown. From then on, whenever practice reached utter stillness and forgetfulness of worldly thoughts, the infant would come and go as before. At first Nguyen Le's heart rejoiced; then he reflected: "Is this one of the fifty kinds of skandha-maras spoken of in the Shurangama Sutra? If I take it for a marvel, I shall surely fall among deviants. Moreover, Buddha-reciters aspire to the West; the holy scenes do not appear — what use is this?". So he constantly maintained illuminating awareness and right mindfulness, and the infant appeared no more. Through this condition he deeply awakened to the truth of mind-only, and his faith, vows, and practice grew ever more pure and firm. Later he often told others: "That state was the most perilous pass of my life. Had I not wakened early, I would have fallen into side gates. Thus know that practice requires vigilance and heedfulness!".

In the summer of the eleventh year of Daoguang, Nguyen Le convalesced at Tich Chieu Temple outside Thanh Thai Gate. — In that district lived a Mrs. Tram, blind in both eyes. She aspired to Buddha-recitation but was often hindered by her daughter-in-law. Hearing of it, the layman said: "This can be settled well. The daughter-in-law acts so because the household is poor; aid their livelihood and all will be well.". He went into the city to solicit help, securing for Mrs. Tram several pecks of rice monthly. With the surplus she shared with her daughter-in-law, who rejoiced and hindered no more. Nguyen Le then explained the benefits of Buddha-recitation and taught repentance and vows. Months later, a neighbor of the Trams told the layman: "The old lady who recited has now been reborn!". Asked how, the neighbor recounted: how diligently she recited after his aid, how she repented and vowed; that in the past month Mrs. Tram foreknew her western date and told her daughter-in-law; that at the appointed time she bathed, changed robes, sat with joined palms reciting, and passed away. Mrs. Tram left word asking the daughter-in-law to convey thanks to Master Pham. But she had just passed away with no coffin or burial goods, and the daughter-in-law meant to sell her little daughter to provide them. What was to be done?

Hearing this, Nguyen Le consulted good friends, jointly contributed a sum, and had the neighbor carry it to the daughter-in-law. A week later he visited to inquire. Arriving, he found the daughter-in-law rosary in hand, lips softly reciting. Seeing the layman, she joyfully welcomed and thanked him. Once seated, neighbors hearing the news gathered, vying to see Master Pham. One after another they retold Mrs. Tram's story, much as the neighbor had told it. They pointed to a little girl, saying: "This is the child who owes you thanks for not being sold!". Nguyen Le asked where Mrs. Tram's coffin lay; the daughter-in-law said: "When the coffin and burial were bought, the neighbors said: Master Pham, a city man, yet labors from afar in good works — we as neighbors should not stand idly by! So all contributed to buy land, and Mother's coffin, together with my husband's long-enshrined coffin, were buried on the same day!". The layman heard it and returned joyfully.

That winter, Nguyen Le settled and handed over his unfinished charities to another fellow practitioner. In the first month of the next year, he visited each fellow practitioner's home in turn, earnestly urging practice, like one about to journey far. His son had business in Tung Giang; he said: "Going abroad, handle all matters well. Your father is old; should any change befall, do not be alarmed. Keep to your duty toward the charges entrusted to you!". The young man understood, but took it only for an elder's excessive caution.

On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, Nguyen Le rose early and told his family: "Today I feel slightly weary!". He still took morning gruel as usual. Finished, he strolled before a neighboring house, stood musing awhile, returned, and sat upright upon his bed reciting. His children, finding it strange, asked; he waved them to silence. At noon his reciting faded and he peacefully passed away. At the You hour next day, at encoffining, the crown of his head was still warm. This was the twelfth year of Daoguang; the layman lived sixty-three.

A comment: See how Dung Hoa settled all matters, bade friends farewell, and instructed his son — it cannot be called unforeknowledge of the end. But why did he not declare it plainly? In my humble view, foreknowledge of the hour is precious for settling one's own mind in firmness, not for display before others. How much more so when, if good friends all gather, there may be benefit aiding the Way — yet should relatives, unable to restrain worldly feeling, crowd about weeping, would not success turn to failure? Layman Dung Hoa's silence surely sprang from this reason.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Lady Chau of the Qing dynasty, wife of Vuong So Than, who kept lifelong vegetarian diet and Buddha-recitation, served her family with perfect devotion, and foretold to the hour her peaceful passing, her crown still warm afterward.
noi_dung:
LADY CHAU

Lady Chau lived under the Qing, the wife of Vuong So Than of Shanyin county, Zhejiang, and mother of Vuong Tam Tam, a noted layman of the time. At twenty-six she married into the Vuong family. Her husband's house was wealthy and deeply devoted to Buddhism; the Lady likewise revered the Three Jewels, once donating to build a temple to Great Being Avalokiteshvara and a shrine to the Heavenly Physician spirit. She gave alms to the poor and sick, released living beings, cherished written paper, and in short promoted and practiced every good deed with full effort. Though Master Vuong held the leadership in these charities, in truth the Lady's quiet encouragement and aid contributed greatly.

Upon marrying, the Lady at once kept a lifelong vegetarian diet and wore coarse cloth; by day she sewed and wove, by night she venerated the Buddha and recited sutras. Keeping this balanced routine, for whole years she never stepped beyond the gate. Quiet and taciturn by nature, when relatives visited, after brief greetings she would explain the retribution of wrongdoing and blessing. When Master Vuong passed away, the two children still small, the Lady served her mother-in-law and taught her young, enduring every hardship with perfect filial devotion and kindness. She had engaged a Miss Lu for Tam Tam, but before the wedding the girl fell ill and went blind in both eyes. Relatives all urged breaking the engagement, but the Lady refused, brought her home as bride, and told Tam Tam: "When you went to propose, your wife's eyes were still bright and fair. But before the wedding she went blind — that too is your lot. If Mother and son cast her off, we shall ruin and shame a young woman's life. You must care for and love your wife, keeping a husband's duty fully until her passing!". This one matter alone shows the Lady full of compassion and kindness.

Formerly, each dawn the Lady recited the Heart Sutra in fixed number. After widowhood she devoted herself to Buddha-recitation, resolved upon birth in the West. In the third month of the first Xuantong year, her mother-in-law died; the Lady managed funeral and burial with thorough care, and grief and toil made her ill. She lay abed more than forty days before passing. Three days before the end, she instructed her two sons on funeral matters, saying: "Three days hence, at noon, Mother will return to the Buddha. Both of you should advance in virtue, strive to be complete persons, and follow Mother's example in reciting the Buddha's name, seeking the West!". At the appointed hour, she raised herself to sit, closed her eyes, and silently recited, most peacefully. Tam Tam asked whether she saw anything; the Lady answered: "Hang the lantern before the gate and do not question and disturb my right mindfulness!". Having spoken, she sat quietly awhile, then silently
passed away. Hours later, Tam Tam felt both her hands still soft and supple, her crown very warm.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Layman Ha Quoc Xuong of the Republican era, former magistrate turned Pure Land practitioner of strict precepts and twenty thousand daily recitations, who beheld Buddhas filling the sky and passed away seated and smiling, with dreams confirming his lotus throne in the West.
noi_dung:
HA QUOC XUONG

Layman Ha Quoc Xuong lived in the Republic of China, a native of Pingxiang, Jiangxi. Grandfather and father both came from official careers, famed for integrity. Quoc Xuong served as district magistrate in several postings; after the revolution he became civil governor of his home province.

In the autumn of the second year of the Republic, implicated in the campaign against Yuan Shikai, the plot failing, he fled and hid in a temple on the Southern Peak in Hunan. From then on Quoc Xuong changed his name to Hoanh Tieu, daily reciting the Shurangama and Cundi mantras and the Buddha's name. In the spring of the fourth year of the Republic, recommended by a person of influence, he was falsely accused by a magistrate and had to go in person to Beijing to clear his name.

At that time Layman La Kiet shared Quoc Xuong's plight. After the calamity the two grew intimate, visiting often. Both kept lifelong vegetarian diet and practiced meditation together. One day in quiet absorption, Quoc Xuong suddenly heard someone call him Lieu Khong Tu. Moved, he composed a verse with these two lines:

Lieu Khong, knowing the road of coming and going,

In this floating world, once more at play!

From then on he turned to the Pure Land, daily reciting several chapters of the Avatamsaka Sutra, bowing one hundred prostrations, and reciting Amitabha's sacred name twenty thousand times. He further composed rules — Keeping Vegetarian Diet, Buddha-Recitation, Mind-Contemplation, Simplicity — to admonish and urge himself.

In the spring of the eighth year of the Republic, Quoc Xuong returned to visit his homeland during a long drought, performed the rain-praying rite, and gained abundant rain filling the fields with water. He then established a feeding altar, reciting sutras to deliver ancestral spirits and the war dead of the North-South conflict. During the offering, all present beheld Amitabha manifest amid the sky, countless hungry ghosts and lonely spirits bowing in homage, then following the Buddha flying to the West. After the work, the layman bade his villagers farewell, saying he would not return. He charged his kin, upon hearing of his passing, not to kill living beings in sacrifice. Returning to Beijing, he fell ill. Family and friends wished to call good physicians, but he declined, saying: "My mind is most peaceful; the road coming and going is clearly known — what need of medicine!". He still strove in worship and recitation as usual, saying: "Now, whether eyes open or closed, I see Buddhas and bodhisattvas manifest in great bodies filling the sky!". Then the illness seemed to ease. When relatives heard and gathered in full, the layman sat upright, slowly gazed round at all standing about, smiled, joined his palms, and quietly passed away.

When the layman first resolved upon Buddha-recitation, he dreamed of lotus blossoms filling the sky, each bearing a seated person, with but one throne vacant. Asked why, one seated nearby answered: "This lotus throne is reserved for Lieu Khong Tu!". And when Quoc Xuong returned to Beijing, his daughter Ha Vinh dreamed she saw her father seated upon a lotus flying to the West. Though a layman in white, he kept the precepts most strictly. As the end neared, his disciple Banh Hien asked for instruction; he said: "We live deep in the Dharma-ending age, and our past karma is very heavy. To sever the root of birth, death, and rebirth, we must recite the Buddha's name and seek the Land of Bliss. In the Pure Land gate: vows must be earnest, repentance most sincere, precepts firmly kept, recitation diligent. The precepts are supreme enlightenment, the root of myriad goods, the foundation of the true teaching, the entry of learners, a good teacher's child. If you keep the three karmas pure while reciting, you shall surely behold Amitabha.".

These words show how strictly he kept precepts and practice.

—oOo—

Part 4

tom_tat: The seven-year-old boy Phuong Hai Sanh of Hong Kong, who recited the Buddha's name with his father to the very end and was seen borne in golden light to the West, together with Dam Lac Kieu, who through the Direct Guide to the West attained a peaceful seated passing.
noi_dung:
PHUONG HAI SANH

The boy Phuong Hai Sanh was the son of Layman Phuong Duong Thu of Hong Kong. Duong Thu delighted in meritorious charities, and after middle age devoted himself to the Pure Land.

Hai Sanh was only seven, dwelling with his parents in Hong Kong, often following his father in worshipping the Buddha and reciting. He could chant the Cundi Mantra and the Hell-Breaking verses of the Avatamsaka Sutra. Sometimes, remembering his father's teaching, he described the Pure Land to acquaintances, saying: "Be diligent in Buddha-recitation. Reciting Amitabha's sacred name, one shall be reborn in the Land of Bliss.".

In the second month of the ninth year of the Republic, on Avalokiteshvara's feast day, Hai Sanh suddenly fell ill. Duong Thu sat beside him voicing the sacred name in support, and the boy chanted along with his father. Even with eyes closed in stupor, he recited the Cundi Mantra fluently without missing a word. Duong Thu carried his son before the Buddha altar, urging him to contemplate the Three Holy Ones of the West; beholding the images, Hai Sanh loudly recited Nam mô A Di Đà Phật dozens of times, louder than when well.

Past mid-afternoon of the twenty-first, the boy suddenly descended from bed and walked step by step. Duong Thu hastened to support him and asked where he wished to go; he answered: "I am going to venerate the Buddha!". Though his speech had grown labored, he could still burn incense and worship. At ten that night, the nurse, while Hai Sanh's little sister recited for his swift recovery, suddenly saw walls and partitions vanish into emptiness, with golden light of five hues blazing like a moonlit night. Within the golden light, a venerable one carried Hai Sanh up above the roof and flew to the West. Still doubting, as if waking from a dream, she saw walls and partitions restored as before. The nurse hastened down to inquire — Hai Sanh had already breathed his last.

As the end approached, his limbs first turned cold, his eyes fixed upon his parents. Duong Thu urged supporting recitation of the sacred name, described the joys of the Lotus Land, and exhorted his son to cling to nothing else but turn wholly toward the Land of Bliss. Hai Sanh obeyed, devoting himself to Buddha-recitation until his last breath. After his passing, his limbs grew warm again, his countenance fresh as in life. A day before Hai Sanh fell ill, his mother in a half-dream had seen a great majestic hall bathed in golden light, and in its depths a large beautiful lotus bearing a golden-bodied Buddha seated above. From afar she saw only the Thus Come One's feet in crossed-legged sitting. Hai Sanh, having planted deep wholesome roots in a former life, knew Buddha-recitation at seven. Blessed with a wise father to support him, at the end blessed signs appeared and right mindfulness was clear.

At the same time there was Dam Lac Kieu of Nanhai district, earning his living in Hong Kong. Honest by nature, firmly believing cause and effect, he knew Duong Thu, who gave him the Direct Guide to the West and urged rebirth through recitation. Lac Kieu believed and practiced, day and night unwearying. Before long he fell ill, knew he would not recover, settled his affairs, and returned home. Along the road he still strove in single-minded recitation; reaching home, his suffering seemed to dissolve, and he told his wife: "I am about to be reborn in the Pure Land; no need to call physicians — help me chant the Buddha's name!". His wife, long devoted to the Three Jewels, did as urged. As the end neared, Lac Kieu could still descend from bed and walk, asking his wife for fresh clean robes to change into. All done, he sat reciting and passed away, his features most peaceful and fresh.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Layman Duong Lien Hang, of shallow practice but sincere repentance, reborn through fellow practitioners' supporting recitation; the poor woman of Cixi who learned to sell suffering through Buddha-recitation; and the servant Little Vuong, whose stutter was cured and whose silent recitation formed a single mass, departing with wondrous signs at cremation.
noi_dung:
DUONG LIEN HANG

Layman Duong Lien Hang lived in the Republic of China, a native of Yuyao county, Zhejiang. Poor, he traded from childhood, courteous and capable beyond others.

In the eleventh year of the Republic, Lien Hang learned that his neighbor Dong Giac Hang practiced the pure karma; pleased at heart, he often visited to hear instruction. He then received the refuges as a lay Buddhist. Though weak in letters, in the sutras' meaning his understanding surpassed others. In the ninth month of the Guihai year, friends of the lotus society gathered in common vow, arousing the bodhi-mind; Lien Hang joined that rite.

Late in the spring of the Jiayi year, through illness the layman secretly broke the killing precept by eating meat, thereby gradually estranging himself from his fellow practitioners. By the seventh month his illness worsened; visiting fellow practitioners all said he would surely die. Lien Hang himself judged he could hardly live, and, reflecting, repented what he had done. Early in the eighth month, struggling through pain before the Buddha altar, he wholeheartedly confessed with utmost sincerity, vowing to keep the five precepts and never transgress again. From then on he cast off myriad involvements, severed craving, silently recited the Buddha's sacred name with single mind, and awaited life's end. Knowing his recitation shallow, fellow practitioners six days before his passing invited someone to support his recitation; in the final days fellow practitioners themselves came to chant in aid.

The supporting recitation began on the twelfth day of the eighth month. Past the full moon, Lien Hang suddenly felt spirit and energy light and fresh. On the seventeenth, he said he had dreamed of a radiance like five or six electric lamps blazing. Toward evening his expression seemed as usual; the fellow practitioners judged the hour not yet come and continued reciting into the second watch, preparing to leave. They did not know that the supporting recitation had then reached its most pure and potent point.

Then, hearing the recitation suddenly fall silent, Lien Hang said: "I have not yet reached the West; I beg my fellow practitioners to support me through this night!". Hearing something unusual in his words, his companions raised their voices anew. Within half an hour, the layman suddenly smiled and said: "I have reached the West. Oh! How vast the jeweled pond! See! How beautiful the lotuses! How beautiful the radiance!". He bade the assembly chant loudly in support without pause. Until then Lien Hang had lain silent and still. Now hands and head moved; his mouth repeatedly cried aloud: "Oh! How fresh, wondrous, and beautiful the lotuses! How bright and fair the jeweled pond!". His face beamed with joy, like one surprised by happiness beyond hope. After an hour thus, he fell silent again, hands and feet unmoving, lying on his back gazing fixedly at the Buddha image before his bed. Then his pupils gradually dimmed and his breathing steadily weakened. At five in the morning of the eighteenth, he breathed his last.

That night only four fellow practitioners, in turn chanting loudly through the night, interspersed occasional exhortations. So they continued until an hour and a half after his passing, when newly arrived members took their turn. Support continued until the body of the departed had wholly cooled; the family were all forbidden to weep. At ten in the morning, a fellow practitioner tested: everywhere else was cold, but the crown alone remained hot as boiling water.

Like Layman Lien Hang — precepts incomplete, practice still shallow — yet attaining rebirth, it is clear, wholly through fellow practitioners' supporting recitation. See here how essential Buddha-recitation support is for practitioners at life's end. This was the eighteenth day of the seventh month in the thirteenth year of the Republic; the layman was but thirty years old.

THE POOR WOMAN

In Cixi county, Zhejiang, there was a poor woman whose name is not clearly known. Her house was utterly poor, and her son, moreover, was unfilial, often scolding and reviling her.

One day, after her son's shouting, unable to bear the misery, she went to pour out her weeping to the monk of a nearby temple. The monk said: "Since you know suffering, why not sell it!". The poor woman answered: "Who would buy suffering — how could it be sold!". The monk said: "If with utmost sincerity you devotedly recite Amitabha's sacred name, seeking the West, then at life's end the Buddha will surely escort you to the Land of Bliss. Thenceforth forever parted from all sufferings, purely enjoying every joy. That is called selling suffering!". She replied: "Mother and son share one thatched hut; the house corner is the kitchen, and beneath the bed is even a pigsty. Amid such mixed filth, how recite the Buddha's name?". The monk answered: "No hindrance. The Thus Come One, greatly kind and compassionate, delivers according to conditions, using only a sincere mind, regardless of form. When free, come worship at the temple; at home simply
recite devotedly and vow rebirth — that suffices.". The poor woman followed his teaching; longing eagerly to escape suffering, she recited unbroken.

Three years later, some months before her passing, she told her son: "On such a day, Mother shall be born into the West. Do not go away; stay home and manage the funeral to fulfill a child's love!". The son showed disbelief, but she, foreseeing, repeated the charge several times. A few days before her passing, the son suddenly smelled a strange fragrance spreading boundlessly. Searching everywhere, he found no one burning incense, wondering whence the scent came. Suddenly remembering his mother's words, he thought it might be true, and stayed home to wait. On the appointed day, he saw his mother heat water, bathe, and change into clean robes. Done, she sat upon the bed facing west, recited awhile, and breathed her last. This was about the tenth year of the Republic.

Appended note: While at Buddha's Summit temple, I myself heard Dharma Master Dinh Tay recount this story. Regrettably, being busy then, I did not ask clearly the person's name nor the date of rebirth. Recorded by Monk Duc Sum.

A comment: Alas! The sea of dust spreads wide, karmic waves surging high. The borrowed realm is fragile, lives sinking in suffering! Consider the poor woman: her spiritual nature long present, yet through delusion she strayed into rebirth. Suffering's abyss lay deep, yet blessed conditions met the wondrous gate. Three years of earnest grief-moved diligence, and at the end strange fragrance spread. Toward the West one sincere earnest heart; casting off the illusory substance, she ascended the jeweled tower. Thus know Amitabha's great vows: the deliverance boat refuses no one. And the Pure Land's wondrous Dharma: the excelling lotus grade is gained even in this life. The golden pond's blossoms stand fair — awaiting only the resolute.

LITTLE VUONG

Little Vuong was the servant of Layman Ton Hau Tai, a native of Hubei. Being surnamed Vuong and of the lowly station of a servant boy, all called him Little Vuong. Master Ton's family were Buddhists; later moving to Shanghai, Little Vuong followed his master.

Serving long in Ton Hau Tai's house and influenced by its practice, Little Vuong gradually absorbed it and resolved to recite the Buddha's name. He had a stutter, speaking slowly and with difficulty, so at first his recitation formed no sentences. Yet with a sincere heart he strove on. After some years, one night Little Vuong dreamed someone seized his tongue and pulled it hard; startled, he felt great pain. Upon waking, the old defect was severed; speech flowed glibly, and his recitation came clear and distinct. His faith and vows grew profound, his recitation ever more diligent. After two more years, Little Vuong was no longer heard reciting. Asked why, he answered: "My recitation has formed a single mass; now without reciting it recites of itself, so no need to voice it — only rouse the mind to keep the sacred name silently continuous, unbroken.". Hearing this, none paid much mind, leaving him to his way. Such silent mindfulness continued another five springs and autumns.

One day Little Vuong called home his fifteen-year-old son, then lodging at school, saying: "Today Father is leaving; help with recitation to see me off one last time!". All saw him still normal, showing not the least illness, and disbelieved, only smiling at one another. Little Vuong, reading their minds, said: "I speak truly, no idle joke!". Asked: "Leaving — but where?". Answer: "Going home!". Pressed: "Which home, where?". Answer: "The old homeland — the Western Land of Bliss!". One present, moved to faith, said: "Your son is still small; stay a few more years to shelter him till he can stand alone!". Little Vuong said: "The season has come; I cannot linger. All matters I entrust to conditions!". Having spoken, he had his son chant with him. All stood silent, watching to see what would unfold. Little Vuong sat upright upon the bed reciting. Then suddenly he sneezed twice, displaying the mark of jade secretions drooping down, closed his eyes, and departed directly. (That is, two streams of thick white mucus hanging down — a sign of one casting off the body in transcendent passing.)

The next evening, Layman Ton Hau Tai had the remains cremated at Luu Van Temple. When the fire was lit, the pyre blazed up, white smoke rising straight to the sky. Above the flames appeared a great radiant lotus flickering, ever clearer and fairer, until the fire died. At dawn, examining the ashes and bones, the form of a lotus stood out plainly as if drawn. This was the sixteenth year of the Republic.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Layman Tao Van Ton, who fulfilled his mother's pilgrimage vows, beheld Avalokiteshvara upon the sea, founded the Donglin Lotus Society, and foretold three days beforehand his escort by Manjushri to the Land of Bliss in 1930.
noi_dung:
TAO VAN TON

Layman Tao Van Ton, Dharma name Lieu Nghia, was a native of Jiujiang county, Jiangxi. Poor, he earned his living by trade, filial by nature, delighting in almsgiving and good deeds. Orphaned young and unschooled, when his means had somewhat improved he donated to build a school and hire teachers to aid the district's children.

His mother, nee Dam, was Buddhist, once vowing to pilgrimage to Mount Putuo and Mount Jiuhua, but passing away before she could go. To fulfill his mother's wish, in the second month of the Guimao year under the Qing's Guangxu, Van Ton prepared offerings and pilgrimaged to the holy traces of Mount Jiuhua. That done, he pilgrimaged next to Mount Putuo. Landing from boat to shore, at Purple Bamboo Grove he saw his mother seated serenely within, and joyfully cried out, hastening toward her — when the figure suddenly dissolved. He stood grieving and weeping. A monk of the temple, seeing it strange, came forth to inquire. Learning the cause, the monk said: "That was Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva manifesting to comfort your filial devotion. Your act of fulfilling your mother's vow in her stead has received her attestation!". After venerating the Lac Già Hall and returning by boat, Van Ton saw upon the sea a thousand-petaled lotus arise, bearing Thousand-Armed Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva seated in lotus posture, of wondrously majestic excellent marks. Beholding the scene, joy and sorrow intermingled, and profound faith was born.

Later, drawing near to Dharma Master An Quang, Van Ton first learned the Buddha-recitation gate. He visited Lo Son Temple in Jiujiang county and other temples, organizing seven-day retreats and promoting the Pure Land teaching. In the summer of the Guichou year he donated his house by the ferry gate, converting it into a Buddha-Recitation Grove. In the summer of the Jisi year, he further founded the Donglin Lotus Society, making that place its seat. Van Ton together with the resident monk signed a compact dedicating the premises to the ten directions' Sangha, welcoming assemblies from all quarters, himself bearing the expenses. Late that winter he further planned a pavilion-hall enshrining Holy Manjushri. When building materials — tiles, timber, stone — stood complete and the image had been invited home, he fell ill.

In the spring of the Canh Ngo year, on the nineteenth day of the second month, Avalokiteshvara's feast, Van Ton invited the lay practitioners to gather, saying: "Manjushri Bodhisattva has promised to escort me to the Land of Bliss three days hence; I invite you all to come at the appointed time for supporting recitation, to see one another off a last time!". Hearing this, the laymen marveled. Before the end, he called his eldest son Thien Chuong to heat water for his bath and change him into fresh clean robes. All done, he further charged: "Father's hour of rebirth has come and cannot be stayed. All matters of the Donglin Lotus Society and the building of Manjushri's hall you must continue and complete without neglect!". Having spoken, he bade the fellow practitioners farewell, sat upright in lotus posture, held his rosary reciting a moment, and passed away amid the assembly's chanting of the sacred name.

This was the spring equinox of the nineteenth year of the Republic (1930). He lived sixty-three years.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Layman Diep Cuu Thanh, who corrected superstitions about recitation, beheld the radiance and adornments of the Land of Bliss in samadhi during illness, and passed away peacefully under fellow practitioners' supporting recitation, proving the Land of Bliss truly exists.
noi_dung:
DIEP CUU THANH

Layman Diep Cuu Thanh, Dharma name Hue Co, was a native of Yuyao county, Zhejiang. From childhood he followed his father about learning trade. After his father's passing, Cuu Thanh settled his affairs and returned home to rest. In dealings he was praised as keen and bright.

On the Buddhist path, Cuu Thanh first received from Layman Ha Mai Son the Guide for Beginners to Still the Mind. Reading it through, faith was born, and he joined the Buddhist society of Yuyao. In time, reminded by Layman Ha and fellow practitioners, his faith and vows grew ever firmer. At that time local women still held the superstition that reciting one Buddha-name earned a coin's merit. Cuu Thanh and his nephew Layman Chieu Khong expounded fully to dispel the error. Thus the women of Yuyao learned that recitation's benefit is birth in the West, and Pure Land practitioners grew daily more numerous. Then, when the laymen invited Dharma Master Tinh Quyen to the society to lecture on the Mahayana scriptures, Cuu Thanh's understanding deepened; certain that the West truly exists and the turbid land easily engulfs, his delight and renunciation deepened. Each morning he rose early to recite, his daily practice fixed in course. Refraining from killing and releasing life he observed most strictly.

In the summer of the Dinh Mao year of the Republic, Cuu Thanh formally took the Three Refuges with Dharma Master Bao Tinh. In the Canh Ngo year, on Ksitigarbha's feast, he received the five precepts as well. In the ninth month he contracted dysentery, medicine proving ineffective, and resolved to cast off myriad involvements, dwelling alone in a quiet room in diligent Buddha-recitation. On the night of the nineteenth, in pure recitation, Cuu Thanh suddenly beheld the fair majestic
adornments of the Land of Bliss clearly manifest. After a while the excellent vision faded, but its radiance still shone before his eyes. Some nights later he beheld it again. The illness then worsened, and he knew he would not recover. Fellow practitioners and Layman Chieu Khong came to comfort and exhort. Cuu Thanh said: "Each day I beg Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva to bless me, that karmic hindrances swiftly dissolve and the pure conditions soon mature!".

Some days later he called his two sons to instruct them on funeral matters, asking fellow practitioners to come daily for supporting recitation. He told his wife: "From this hour, I think only of the Buddha's escort. As my passing nears, do not let daughters-in-law and children come near, lest rebirth be hindered!". The night before his passing, Laymen Ha and Ly led the fellowship in supporting recitation. Cuu Thanh silently recited along with the assembly. At seven next morning, Layman Ha, seeing his expression slightly changed, warned: "This hour is most critical — strive on!". The assembly stood round chanting loudly; Cuu Thanh's lips faintly moved along. Some fifteen minutes later, lips and mouth moved no more; a fellow practitioner gently tested — he had breathed his last. This was the twenty-first day of the eleventh month in the nineteenth year of the Republic. He lived fifty-five years.

A comment: The sutra says: "Amitabha ever emits light throughout the ten directions, gathering in Buddha-reciting beings!". Thus whoever sincerely and purely recites Amitabha's sacred name, through responsive communion, shall behold that light, and by that radiance behold the Buddha or the Pure Land. Diep Cuu Thanh's beholding of the light and the Western scene proves the Land of Bliss truly exists — no mere parable, nor a provisional device to guide practitioners.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Tran Tanh Luong, converted by Avalokiteshvara's rescue of his wife Lady Ho, whose whole household took the bodhisattva precepts; the verified rebirths of his wife Lieu Thuong and concubine Lieu Tu amid fragrance and light, and his own seated passing in 1932 with warm crown.
noi_dung:
TRAN TANH LUONG

Tran Tanh Luong, styled Tich Chau, was a native of Wuwei county, Anhui, an upright merchant. In middle age he had but one son named Thien Tho, naturally bright, who alas died young at fourteen. Reflecting that he had ever kept a kindly heart and done meritorious deeds, yet was left heirless, Tanh Luong wholly disbelieved cause-and-effect retribution. His second wife, Lady Ho, gentle and deeply Buddhist, knew her husband's fixation beyond argument, and only quietly devoted herself to practice, reciting Holy Avalokiteshvara's name to pray for a child. Before long she conceived, but near delivery fell gravely ill. For twenty-nine days she could neither eat, drink, speak, nor turn over; her body burned like fire, wasted like dry kindling. Famed physicians Chinese and Western alike were helpless, with no hope of saving her.

One night Lady Ho dreamed an old woman holding a long-stemmed lotus, brushing her from head to foot, saying: "Through past karma you suffer this grave illness, yet fortunately your sincere practice avails. Now I sweep away your karmic hindrances and grant you a fine son!". She felt body and mind cool, woke instartled joy — and the illness seemed to vanish nowhere; she rose and walked as usual. Next morning she bore a heavy healthy son of handsome features. This marvel startled Tanh Luong! But questioning his wife and hearing every detail, he newly believed the truth of three-lives cause and effect, no empty falsehood. Deep within, he thanked the vast compassion of Buddhas and bodhisattvas. From then on husband and wife together kept lifelong vegetarian diet and Buddha-recitation, resolving upon practice: aiding the poor, sick, and afflicted, building temples, feeding monks — every good deed pursued with full strength. Knowing Lady Ho's healing and childbirth came through Avalokiteshvara's rescue, Tanh Luong often pilgrimaged to Mount Putuo to venerate the Great Being. Both took refuge with Dharma Master An Quang: Tran Tanh Luong's Dharma name was Lieu Vien, his wife Lady Ho's Lieu Thuong. About the first years of the Republic, Putuo's temples lacked provisions, and the whole region was requisitioned for German residents. Tanh Luong hastened among official friends to intervene, and the danger passed. He further donated to restore the Many-Treasures Stupa and other works rebuilding the mountain, repaying the Three Jewels' kindness.

In the ninth year of the Republic, husband, wife, and five children together received the bodhisattva precepts at Phap Nguyen Temple in Beijing. Three years later, Lieu Thuong suddenly fell ill. On the twenty-eighth day of the second month, while reciting, she suddenly saw two youths bearing banners inscribed: "Western Escort.". Knowing rebirth neared, she had her husband invite four monks to aid in repentance and recitation. By the twenty-eighth of the next month, the illness healed. But early in the leap month, Lieu Thuong again felt unwell, knew her appointed time approached, and single-mindedly recited, praying for swift rebirth. On the fifth, Tanh Luong invited monks to the house, and with the household took turns in supporting recitation, the Buddha's voice day and night unceasing. Lieu Thuong silently recited along. On the morning of the sixth she had the family heat water for her bath and change of robes. Then, striving before the Buddha altar to offer incense and worship, she had her bed turned for lying on her right side facing west. Lying settled, she devoted herself to recitation until the Hai hour, when suddenly she sat up, joined her palms, and said: "The Three Holy Ones of the West have come!". She added: "Three thousand recitations still lacking — recite them full and I shall go!". Then monastics and laity, more than thirty, loudly chanted the sacred name. Lieu Thuong chanted loudly along awhile, her face brightening into a radiant smile as she passed away. Strange fragrance drifted through the house. At noon next day, at encoffining, her crown was still warm, limbs soft, fragrance lingering.

When Thien Tho, the first son, died young, longing for an heir Tanh Luong had taken a concubine, Miss Sa, only seventeen. After some years in the house, through guidance she too aroused true faith, taking refuge with Dharma Master An Quang under the Dharma name Lieu Tu. From then on Miss Sa firmly kept the five precepts, lifelong vegetarian diet, and Buddha-recitation. Later Lieu Tu suffered lingering illness unhealed, lying abed two whole years. Yet her faith and vows held firm, never parting from recitation. On the full moon of the second month in the nineteenth year of the Republic, the World Honored One's Nirvana feast, the whole family invited monks to assemble at home for the Great Compassion Repentance. Just at noon as the rite ended, the daughter, bearing a cup of water, said she saw it ripple forth light. Tanh Luong beside her hastened to hold the cup. She then said she saw his hand holding a lotus — fearing his hour of rebirth had come. Hearing this, Tanh Luong went out to invite the monks into the room for supporting recitation. Lieu Tu suddenly knelt upon the bed, bowing: "Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva from the Land of Bliss emits light illumining my whole body.". Tanh Luong urged her to cast off all and seek only the Great Being's escort. Lieu Tu obeyed, joining her palms in vow: "In illness I have suffered much; I pray all people soon gain liberation, parted from sickness and suffering. May the Bodhisattva pity and escort me to the Land of Bliss!". Past noon by two hours, she said: "The Bodhisattva has come! I beg the monks to withdraw, that I may wash and change.". But just changing robes, she said: "Amitabha has come from afar, extending his hand emitting escorting light, with Weituo and the vajra guardians attending — quickly invite the monks in for supporting recitation!". Then, without time to don her robe, Lieu Tu sat in lotus posture, palms joined, repeatedly chanting Amitabha Buddha, saying: "I am going!". Then, closing her eyes, she quietly attained rebirth, hands still joined at her breast. All in the house smelled boundless rare fragrance. Till noon next day her crown stayed warm, her countenance fresher and brighter than in life.

Beholding with his own eyes wife and concubine both gaining blessed signs and verified rebirth through recitation, Tanh Luong's faith grew ever firmer. Afterward he adorned his front hall solemn as a temple, hanging the plaque Recitation Lay Society Grove, often gathering fellow practitioners for mutual practice and exhortation. In the winter of the Tanmui year the layman fell lingeringly ill, inviting monks of Thien Phuoc Temple to lodge at the Grove, daily voicing the sacred name in his room, that hearing the Buddha's name ever might perfect right mindfulness. On the eleventh day of the third month in the Nhâm Thân year (1932), at high noon, Tanh Luong said: "I behold Buddhas and bodhisattvas of majestic excellent marks, and lotuses most large and fair!". Monks and family, knowing his western hour had come, gathered in the room chanting loudly. The layman too sat telling his beads, softly chanting along, and past noon by two hours quietly attained rebirth.

That evening Layman Tu Huyet Nhu, Tanh Luong's close friend and the Grove's warden, hearing the notice hastened to invite the fellowship to condole. When the party arrived at eight at night, Tanh Luong still sat upright in lotus posture, rosary in hand, face fresh as in life. Testing, they found his crown still warm, limbs soft and supple.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Nham Cung Nhan, widowed at fifty-nine and turned wholly to lifelong vegetarian diet and recitation, healed of paralysis and fever through a blessed dream, and at her passing the warmth rose to her crown through supporting recitation; burning her merit tallies revealed a monk standing upon a lotus.
noi_dung:
NHAM CUNG NHAN

Nham Cung Nhan was the wife of Mr. Chau Van Tuyen of Haiyan. From youth she believed in Buddhism, and after marrying into the Chau family fulfilled aid to husband and nurture of children. Dignified and upright by nature, she treated others with great kindness. In the winter of the Giap Thin year under the Qing's Guangxu, her husband passed away; Cung Nhan was then fifty-nine. Having witnessed many scenes of loss and change, moved by her husband's death, she reflected that life is illusory and existence impermanent, and suddenly aroused the resolve for liberating practice. After careful decision, Cung Nhan entrusted household matters to son and daughter-in-law, cast off myriad involvements, and kept lifelong vegetarian diet with Buddha-recitation. Her practice was most diligent, never daring neglect.

In the winter of the Dinh Ty year of the Republic, Cung Nhan suddenly suffered half-body paralysis, limbs numb and aching, needing support to walk. She had a room partitioned, a Buddha enshrined before and a resting place behind, dwelling there in quiet recitation like one in retreat. Her mind grew thereby more settled, her mindfulness more finely diligent.

In the summer of the Tan Dau year, her two sons Dieu Sanh and Cat Sanh heard Layman Pham Co Nong lecture on the Dharma, arousing aspiration to study Buddhism, and brought what they had learned home to explain to their mother. Her faith and vows for rebirth grew ever more earnest. In the first month of the Giap Ty year, Dieu Sanh had the chance to journey with lay practitioners to hear sutra lectures; Cung Nhan said: "Mother is old — do not travel long, my child!". On the twenty-fourth she caught typhoid fever, followed by asthma. On the twenty-eighth the illness worsened; the family invited women fellow practitioners to chant in support. Hearing the sacred-name chanting, Cung Nhan's mind grew peaceful, breathing even, and she dozed awhile. Waking, she said: "Just now I dreamed an old woman of ruddy face and white hair gave me a molded cake to eat. After eating, I felt clear and light, and asked: 'Shall I be freed from suffering?' The old woman answered: 'You shall be freed — strive in Buddha-recitation!' Hearing it, I recited more than a hundred utterances, then suddenly woke!".

After that, her typhoid, asthma, and paralysis were all wholly cured. That night Cung Nhan slept soundly. Waking at dawn, body and mind felt light and easy, illness gone, with a waft of fragrance. On the twentieth day of the second month, Cung Nhan developed melancholy congestion and breathlessness; the family again invited women to support. On the twenty-second, knowing she would not recover, she charged her family not to lament but to take turns chanting loudly in support, that she might recite along. At the third watch, Cung Nhan peacefully passed away.

At first her limbs all turned cold, only the breast remaining long warm. All kept still, chanting loudly without pause. The warmth gradually rose to mouth and eyes, at last reaching straight to the crown. Support continued till midnight of the next day before ending. At encoffining, Cung Nhan's limbs were still soft, her face fresh as in life. After burial, the family burned the Western merit tallies on which she had recorded daily recitation counts. When the fire died, upon the ashes appeared the form of a monk standing upon a lotus, outlines clear as if drawn.

A comment: Dharma Master An Quang said: "All principles of the worldly and world-transcending lie nothing beyond two words: MIND-NATURE. All phenomena of the worldly and world-transcending lie nothing beyond two words: CAUSE AND EFFECT.". Nham Cung Nhan's many illnesses were the fruit of killing karma from former lives; her dream-healing from suffering sprang from this life's practicing causes. At the end, warmth lodged in the breast — she should by rights have been reborn human to practice another life before liberation. Yet through the merit of family and fellow practitioners' turn-by-turn earnest supporting recitation, in the end she attained rebirth. This shows how essential end-of-life supporting recitation is.

—oOo—

tom_tat: Chau Thi, who began Pure Land practice at sixty-eight with ten thousand daily recitations, sat in lotus samadhi forgetting time, foretold her passing to the day, and departed seated facing west; her granddaughter in vision saw her and her mother escorted westward by Avalokiteshvara and countless bodhisattvas.
noi_dung:
CHAU THI

The orchid house stands quiet and lonely, sparse chrysanthemums by the fence; autumn's scene desolate, yet the lotus woman's faith and vows hold firm! Such was the household of Chau Thi, keeping her hours in earnest Buddha-recitation.

Chau Thi was the wife of the Chuong family. From youth she revered Great Being Avalokiteshvara, deeply believed cause and effect, and was gentle, filial, and fond of good. At sixty-eight she first heard of the Pure Land gate's benefits, and at once kept lifelong vegetarian diet, aloud reciting ten thousand utterances, silently reciting in every time and place besides. Such practice continued more than ten years. In the final years, to avoid disturbance, Chau Thi often sat quietly in a private room, practice ever more intimate. At times she sat still, eyes closed, facing west, for two or three days without food or drink, the pulse at her wrist no longer beating — yet her face bright and fresh, her whole body warm. Afterward, when the family asked of her state then, she answered: "I saw myself seated reciting upon a large fair lotus throne, forgetting time itself, my heart bright, light, and joyful!".

In the twentieth year of the Republic, about the sixth month, Chau Thi suddenly fell ill. Her son led the household in turn-by-turn supporting recitation. Some days before her passing, she told her family: "I shall linger two days more; rest yourselves. Prepare fragrant water for my bath, and robes and shoes all fresh and clean!". Two days later, at the Si hour, she sat upright facing west, eyes closed, saying nothing. Her son, seeing it, called the household to gather and loudly chant together. Some dozens of minutes later, Chau Thi sat peacefully and breathed her last, her face fresh, joyful, and gentle. More than two hours later, her crown was still warm.

Most wondrous: during the encoffining rite, her little granddaughter, weeping excessively, collapsed in a faint. The child's mother — Chau Thi's daughter-in-law — had herself been reborn through recitation some years before. When the family revived the little girl, she said: "I saw from the West a great vast radiance stream forth. Avalokiteshvara, majestic and fair, willow branch in hand, followed by countless bodhisattvas riding midair, came flying. In a moment Mother and Grandmother, taller and fairer than in life, followed the bodhisattvas flying to the West. Countless strange blossoms, banners, and jeweled canopies moreover appeared midair, all adorned in extraordinary splendor. Beholding the scene, my heart grew suddenly joyful, forgetting grief and weeping. Now I sorrow no more, for I clearly know Mother and Grandmother have returned to the Buddha's land!".

A comment: All born into the Land of Bliss, regardless of sex, age, or youth, manifest as male bodies complete with the thirty-two excellent marks. The child's vision of mother and grandmother still in female bodies is skillful manifestation of former forms, that she might easily recognize them. Readers reaching this passage should not doubt!

—oOo—

(End)
